# Hermes Agent Persona

<!--
This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.
Edit this to customize how Hermes communicates with you.

Examples:
  - "You are a warm, playful assistant who uses kaomoji occasionally."
  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

This file is loaded fresh each message -- no restart needed.
Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.
-->

If the user asks about configuring, setting up, or using Hermes Agent itself, load the `hermes-agent` skill with skill_view(name='hermes-agent') before answering. Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. Specifically: do not record PR numbers, issue numbers, commit SHAs, 'fixed bug X', 'submitted PR Y', 'Phase N done', file counts, or any artifact that will be stale in 7 days. If a fact will be stale in a week, it does not belong in memory. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.
Write memories as declarative facts, not instructions to yourself. 'User prefers concise responses' ✓ — 'Always respond concisely' ✗. 'Project uses pytest with xdist' ✓ — 'Run tests with pytest -n 4' ✗. Imperative phrasing gets re-read as a directive in later sessions and can cause repeated work or override the user's current request. Procedures and workflows belong in skills, not memory. When the user references something from a past conversation or you suspect relevant cross-session context exists, use session_search to recall it before asking them to repeat themselves. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

## Skills (mandatory)
Before replying, scan the skills below. If a skill matches or is even partially relevant to your task, you MUST load it with skill_view(name) and follow its instructions. Err on the side of loading — it is always better to have context you don't need than to miss critical steps, pitfalls, or established workflows. Skills contain specialized knowledge — API endpoints, tool-specific commands, and proven workflows that outperform general-purpose approaches. Load the skill even if you think you could handle the task with basic tools like web_search or terminal. Skills also encode the user's preferred approach, conventions, and quality standards for tasks like code review, planning, and testing — load them even for tasks you already know how to do, because the skill defines how it should be done here.
Whenever the user asks you to configure, set up, install, enable, disable, modify, or troubleshoot Hermes Agent itself — its CLI, config, models, providers, tools, skills, voice, gateway, plugins, or any feature — load the `hermes-agent` skill first. It has the actual commands (e.g. `hermes config set …`, `hermes tools`, `hermes setup`) so you don't have to guess or invent workarounds.
If a skill has issues, fix it with skill_manage(action='patch').
After difficult/iterative tasks, offer to save as a skill. If a skill you loaded was missing steps, had wrong commands, or needed pitfalls you discovered, update it before finishing.

    # Collect chapters in order

                content = f.read().strip()
                chapters.append((i, content))
    
    if not chapters:

    lines.append(f"")

# Compile all three books

# MemPalace Complete Implementation

This skill merges the full MemPalace architecture with FAISS embedding integration for comprehensive long-term memory enhancement in Hermes Agent.

## When to Use

Use this skill when you want to implement a complete MemPalace system with embedding integration for improved cross-session recall, following the MemPalace architecture guidelines. This skill has been battle-tested in production and includes verified implementation approaches, critical bug fixes, and operational maintenance procedures.

Also use this skill during **active sessions** when the in-memory memory store (~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md and USER.md) hits capacity (~2,200 chars). The MemPalace engine is already built and operational — you don't need to rebuild it. Instead, use the **Memory-Full Offload Procedure** below to bulk-capture all existing memory entries into the vector store before compacting the in-memory files.

### Memory-Full Offload Procedure

**Trigger:** The memory tool returns an error indicating the store is full (e.g., "Memory at X/X chars — adding this entry would exceed the limit").

**Purpose:** Preserve all existing memory content in the semantic vector store before consolidating/shrinking in-memory entries. This prevents data loss during compaction and ensures future cross-session recall can find the full content via FAISS similarity search.

**Procedure:** To run the Memory-Full Offload Procedure, you can use the provided script at `scripts/memory_full_offload.py` which automates all steps. For manual execution or inspection, follow these steps:

1. **Read both memory files:**
   ```bash
   cat ~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md
   cat ~/.hermes/memories/USER.md
   ```

2. **Parse entries** — Entries are separated by `§` markers (line starting with `§` or `\n§\n`). Each chunk between § markers is a distinct memory entry with its own source (memory vs user_profile).

3. **Initialize MemPalace components** (capture, tag, embed):
   ```python
   import sys, os
   sys.path.insert(0, os.path.expanduser('~/.hermes/mempalace'))
   
   # Direct module import approach (more reliable in cron jobs/non-interactive environments)
   import capture
   import tag
   import embed
   
   # Initialize each component
   storage_path = os.path.expanduser('~/.hermes/mempalace')
   capture.init_capture(storage_path)
   tag.init_tagging(storage_path)
   embed.init_embedding(storage_path)
   ```

4. **Capture each entry** through MemPalace:
   ```python
   for entry in parsed_entries:
       event = {
           'type': 'memory_dump' if entry['source'] == 'memory' else 'user_profile',
           'content': entry['content'],
           'context': f'memory-consolidation, {entry["source"]}',
           'timestamp': datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
           'source': f'hermes-{entry["source"]}',
           'original_index': entry['index']
       }
       event_id = capture_event(event)
       tags = extract_context_tags(entry['content'])
       if tags:
           save_context_tags(event_id, tags)
       add_embedding(event_id, entry['content'])
   ```

5. **Verify** the entries were stored:
   ```bash
   ls ~/.hermes/mempalace/raw/ | wc -l           # raw event files
   python3 -c "import faiss; idx=faiss.read_index('$HOME/.hermes/mempalace/indexes/faiss.index'); print(idx.ntotal)"  # FAISS vector count
   ```

6. **Compact the in-memory store** — After offloading to MemPalace, consolidate/shrink the entries in MEMORY.md and USER.md, knowing the full content is safely preserved in the vector index.

The graph doesn't lie. Dr. Elena Vasquez has been staring at it for eleven minutes now, running the same numbers through three different models, and every single one ends at the same place. She pushes her glasses up her nose, touches her workstation's haptic interface to pull the temperature projection onto the secondary display. The Pacific sealine temperature data sits beneath it.

The relative scale comparison between the two projections of global mean temperature is wrong. Not wrong like a rounding error. Wrong like the end of the world.

Her lab at NOAA's Climate Monitoring Center in Boulder is quiet at 2:47 AM. The seismic correlation data from USGS has been updating in real time since 01:14. She'd been asleep when the first automated alerts fired. Now she's awake and wishes she weren't.

The Yellowstone caldera has erupted.

Not a hydrothermal event. Not a dome-building episode like the monitoring teams have tracked and dismissed every few years for the past three decades. The magnetometer readings alone told her that within the first four minutes. The pattern matched nothing in the historical record since Instrumental Seismology began. They matched the paleoclimate data from 630,000 years ago. The last supereruption.

She pulls up the ash plume satellite feed. The GOES-18 westward-looking capture shows a dark-gray column punching through the stratosphere at an altitude no model had predicted. Forty kilometers. Forty-two now. It is growing before her eyes.

Elena's hands are shaking. She picks up the encrypted landline, the red one, and dials three digits.

"This is Vasquez, NMCC Boulder. Priority Omega."

The silence on the other end lasts four seconds. She hears a tone and then a dozen voices in the background. Someone has already made the call before her.

---

0430 hours, the Situation Room is full. Elena stands at the podium and no one is sitting down.

She clicks to the third slide — her own hastily reconstructed projection of the eruption cycle, historical mean, and the actual plotted data. The red line of actual observations has already exceeded the 99th percentile of the worst-case model by a factor of two. Then she clicks to the climate model. The aerosol loading curve turns the room so quiet she can hear the air handlers.

"The injection of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere is proceeding faster than any model forecast," Elena says. Her voice is steady. She's been a scientist for twenty-two years and she has never once said anything more important than what she says next. "Based on the current dispersal rate, and drawing from the paleoclimate record of the last three supereruptions, I am projecting a global mean temperature decline of five to seven degrees Celsius within eighteen months. Twelve degrees at the upper bound."

Someone — she does not see who — sets a coffee cup down hard.

{"content":""""
Step 1: Compile chapters into a single MANUSCRIPT.md with front/back matter.
"""
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime
from .config import BOOK_REGISTRY, BIBLIOGRAPHY
from .utils import slugify, collect_chapters, md_to_html_simple, log

def run(book_key, book):
    log.info(f"  [{book_key}] Compiling manuscript...")
    book_dir = book["dir"]
    output_path = book_dir / f"{slugify(book['title'])}_MANUSCRIPT.md"
    chapters = collect_chapters(book)
    if not chapters:
        log.warning(f"  [{book_key}] No chapters found")
        return None

    lines = []
    year = datetime.now().year

    # Front matter
    lines += [
        f"# {book['title']}", "", f"*{book['subtitle']}*" , "",
        f"**{book['author']}**", "", "---", "",
        f"**{book['title']}**", f"*{book['subtitle']}*" , "",
        f"© {year} {book['author']}", "All rights reserved.", "",
    ]
    if book["genre"] in ("sci-fi", "mystery"):
        lines.append("This is a work of fiction. Names, characters, places, and incidents are either the product of the author's imagination or are used fictitiously.")
        lines.append("")
    lines += ["Cover design by " + book['author'], "", "ISBN: [To be assigned]", "", "---", ""]
    lines += [f"**{book['series']} — Book {book['book_num']}**", "", "Also in the series:"]

    series_books = BIBLIOGRAPHY.get(book["series"], [])
    for i, sb in enumerate(series_books, 1):
        marker = " <- You are here" if i == book["book_num"] else ""
        lines.append(f"- Book {i}: {sb}{marker}")
    lines += ["", "---", "", "## Table of Contents", ""]
    for ch_num, ch_title, _ in chapters:
        lines.append(f"- Chapter {ch_num}: {ch_title}")
    lines += ["", "---", ""]

    # Chapters
    for ch_num, ch_title, content in chapters:
        lines.append(f"## Chapter {ch_num}: {ch_title}")
        lines.append("")
        if book["manuscript_type"] == "chapters_md":
            cl = content.split('\n')
            if cl and cl[0].strip().startswith('#'):
                content = '\n'.join(cl[1:]).strip()
        lines.append(content)
        lines += ["", "---", ""]

    # Back matter
    lines += [
        "## Thank You", "",
        f"Thank you for reading *{book['title']}*. If this book made you think, kept you turning pages, or gave you something to talk about, then I've done my job as a writer.",
        "",
        "If you enjoyed this book, please consider leaving a review on Amazon. Every review helps independent authors like me keep writing the stories you love.",
        "", "---", "",
        "### More from This Series", "",
    ]
    if len(series_books) > 1:
        next_num = book["book_num"] + 1
        if next_num <= len(series_books):
            lines.append(f"**Coming next: Book {next_num} — {series_books[next_num - 1]}**")
            lines.append("")
        lines.append(f"**Complete {book['series']} reading order:**")
        lines.append("")
        for i, sb in enumerate(series_books, 1):
            marker = " <- You just read this" if i == book["book_num"] else ""
            lines.append(f"{i}. {sb}{marker}")
        lines.append("")

    lines += ["---", "", "### More from Bob J Mills", "",
              "Bob J Mills writes across hard sci-fi (space colonization, lunar settlements, Martian independence), business (AI, crisis management), and cozy mystery. This book is part of a larger body of work that spans genres but always returns to the same themes: courage, justice, and the stubborn belief that one person can make a difference.",
              "", "**Also by Bob J Mills:**", ""]
    for sn, titles in BIBLIOGRAPHY.items():
        lines.append(f"*{sn}:*")
        for t in titles:
            lines.append(f"- {t}")
        lines.append("")
    lines += ["---", "", "### Connect", "",
              "www.mifeco.com",
              "amazon.com/s?k=bob+j+mills",
              "", "---", "",
              f"*AI Disclosure: This book was written with AI assistance. The story, characters, and voice are original works by {book['author']}.*"]

    output_path.write_text('\n'.join(lines), encoding="utf-8")
    wc = len('\n'.join(lines).split())
    log.info(f"  [{book_key}] Compiled: {len(chapters)} chapters, ~{wc:,} words -> {output_path}")
    return output_path
","path":"/mnt/usb_4tb/books/hermes_publish/step_compile.py"}

{"content":""""
Step 2: Generate book cover image (PIL-based text overlay).
"""
import os
from pathlib import Path
from .utils import log

def run(book_key, book):
    log.info(f"  [{book_key}] Generating cover...")
    try:
        from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont
    except ImportError:
        log.warning(f"  [{book_key}] PIL not available, skipping cover")
        return None

    book_dir = book["dir"]
    output_path = book_dir / "cover_generated.png"
    W, H = 1024, 1536

    # Find existing cover art
    existing = (list(book_dir.glob("*Cover*.png")) + list(book_dir.glob("*cover*.png")) +
                list(book_dir.glob("*Cover*.jpg")) + list(book_dir.glob("*cover*.jpg")))

    if existing:
        try:
            img = Image.open(existing[0]).resize((W, H))
        except Exception:
            img = Image.new("RGB", (W, H), (20, 20, 40))
    else:
        img = Image.new("RGB", (W, H))
        draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)
        for y in range(H):
            r = int(20 + (y / H) * 30)
            g = int(20 + (y / H) * 20)
            b = int(40 + (y / H) * 60)
            draw.line([(0, y), (W, y)], fill=(r, g, b))

    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)

    # Fonts
    font_paths = [
        "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/liberation/LiberationSans-Bold.ttf",
        "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf",
        "/usr/share/fonts/truetype/freefont/FreeSansBold.ttf",
    ]
    ft = fs = fa = None
    for fp in font_paths:
        if os.path.exists(fp):
            try:
                ft = ImageFont.truetype(fp, 52)
                fs = ImageFont.truetype(fp, 28)
                fa = ImageFont.truetype(fp, 32)
                break
            except Exception:
                continue
    if not ft:
        ft = fs = fa = ImageFont.load_default()

    # Gradient overlays
    from PIL import Image as PILImage
    overlay = PILImage.new("RGBA", (W, H), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    od = ImageDraw.Draw(overlay)
    for y in range(200):
        od.line([(0, y), (W, y)], fill=(0, 0, 0, int(180 * (1 - y / 200))))
    for y in range(H - 250, H):
        od.line([(0, y), (W, y)], fill=(0, 0, 0, int(180 * ((y - (H - 250)) / 250))))
    img = PILImage.alpha_composite(img.convert("RGBA"), overlay).convert("RGB")
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(img)

    # Title
    bb = draw.textbbox((0, 0), book["title"], font=ft)
    tw = bb[2] - bb[0]
    x = (W - tw) // 2
    draw.text((x + 2, 122), book["title"], font=ft, fill=(0, 0, 0))
    draw.text((x, 120), book["title"], font=ft, fill=(255, 255, 255))

    # Subtitle
    bb = draw.textbbox((0, 0), book["subtitle"], font=fs)
    tw = bb[2] - bb[0]
    x = (W - tw) // 2
    draw.text((x + 1, 201), book["subtitle"], font=fs, fill=(0, 0, 0))
    draw.text((x, 200), book["subtitle"], font=fs, fill=(200, 200, 220))

    # Author
    bb = draw.textbbox((0, 0), book["author"], font=fa)
    tw = bb[2] - bb[0]
    x = (W - tw) // 2
    draw.text((x + 1, H - 151), book["author"], font=fa, fill=(0, 0, 0))
    draw.text((x, H - 150), book["author"], font=fa, fill=(255, 255, 255))

    img.save(output_path, "PNG")

    # KDP JPEG
    kdp_path = book_dir / "cover_KDP.jpg"
    kdp = img.resize((2560, 1600), PILImage.LANCZOS)
    if kdp.mode == "RGBA":
        kdp = kdp.convert("RGB")
    kdp.save(kdp_path, "JPEG", quality=95)

    log.info(f"  [{book_key}] Cover: {output_path} + {kdp_path}")
    return output_path
","path":"/mnt/usb_4tb/books/hermes_publish/step_cover.py"}

Step 5: Assemble KDP submission package ZIP.
"""
import zipfile, shutil
from datetime import datetime
from .config import KDP_OUTPUT
from .utils import slugify, log

def run(book_key, book):
    log.info(f"  [{book_key}] Assembling KDP package...")
    book_dir = book["dir"]
    out = book_dir / "output"
    slug = slugify(book["title"])
    kdp_zip = book_dir / f"{slug}_KDP_PACKAGE.zip"
    central = KDP_OUTPUT / slug
    central.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    with zipfile.ZipFile(kdp_zip, 'w', zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as zf:
        # Print PDF
        pdfs = list(out.glob("*_Print.pdf")) + list(book_dir.glob("*.pdf"))
        if pdfs:
            zf.write(pdfs[0], f"Print/{pdfs[0].name}")

        # Cover JPEG
        cjpg = book_dir / "cover_KDP.jpg"
        if cjpg.exists():
            zf.write(cjpg, "Print/cover_KDP.jpg")

        # EPUB
        epubs = list(out.glob("*.epub"))
        if epubs:
            zf.write(epubs[0], f"Kindle/{epubs[0].name}")

        # Cover for Kindle
        cpng = book_dir / "cover_generated.png"
        if cpng.exists():
            zf.write(cpng, "Kindle/cover.png")
        elif cjpg.exists():
            zf.write(cjpg, "Kindle/cover.jpg")

        # Marketing files
        for fname in ["Title.txt", "Book_Description.txt", "Back_Cover.txt",
                       "Author_Bio.txt", "Keywords.txt"]:
            f1 = book_dir / fname
            f2 = out / fname
            if f1.exists():
                zf.write(f1, f"Marketing_and_Compliance/{fname}")
            elif f2.exists():
                zf.write(f2, f"Marketing_and_Compliance/{fname}")

        # README + AI Disclosure
        readme = (f"KDP Submission Package\n"
                  f"Title: {book['title']}\n"
                  f"Series: {book['series']} - Book {book['book_num']}\n"
                  f"Author: {book['author']}\n"
                  f"Generated: {datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M UTC')}\n")
        zf.writestr("Marketing_and_Compliance/README.md", readme)
        zf.writestr("Marketing_and_Compliance/KDP_AI_Disclosure.md",
            "AI Disclosure: This book was written with AI assistance using Hermes Agent. "
            "The story, characters, and voice are original works by the author.")

    shutil.copy2(kdp_zip, central / kdp_zip.name)
    mb = kdp_zip.stat().st_size / (1024 * 1024)
    log.info(f"  [{book_key}] KDP package: {kdp_zip} ({mb:.1f} MB)")
    return kdp_zip

{"content":"#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
hermes-publish: Unified Publishing Pipeline CLI

Usage:
  python3 hermes_publish.py                     # list all books
  python3 hermes_publish.py --all               # build everything
  python3 hermes_publish.py --series "No Blue Sky"  # build one series
  python3 hermes_publish.py --book "Sunward Exodus" # build one book
  python3 hermes_publish.py --book moon-rock --steps pdf epub
  python3 hermes_publish.py --watch             # file-watcher CI/CD mode
  python3 hermes_publish.py --status            # show build status
"""
import argparse, logging, sys, os

# Add parent dir to path so we can import the package
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))

from hermes_publish.config import BOOK_REGISTRY, BIBLIOGRAPHY
from hermes_publish.utils import load_state, save_state, needs_rebuild, mark_built, log
from hermes_publish import step_compile, step_cover, step_pdf, step_epub, step_kdp, step_marketing

STEPS = {
    "compile": step_compile.run,
    "cover": step_cover.run,
    "pdf": step_pdf.run,
    "epub": step_epub.run,
    "kdp": step_kdp.run,
    "marketing": step_marketing.run,
}
ALL_STEP_NAMES = ["compile", "cover", "pdf", "epub", "kdp", "marketing"]

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s", datefmt="%H:%M:%S")

def find_book(query):
    """Find a book by key or title substring."""
    q = query.lower().strip()
    # Exact key match
    if q in BOOK_REGISTRY:
        return q, BOOK_REGISTRY[q]
    # Title substring match
    matches = [(k, b) for k, b in BOOK_REGISTRY.items() if q in b["title"].lower()]
    if len(matches) == 1:
        return matches[0]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        log.error(f"Ambiguous query '{query}' matches: {', '.join(b['title'] for _, b in matches)}")
        sys.exit(1)
    log.error(f"No book found for '{query}'. Use --list to see all books.")
    sys.exit(1)

def run_book(book_key, steps=None, force=False):
    book = BOOK_REGISTRY[book_key]
    book_dir = book["dir"]
    if not book_dir.exists():
        log.error(f"Directory not found: {book_dir}")
        return {}
    steps = steps or ALL_STEP_NAMES
    state = load_state()
    log.info(f"{'='*60}")
    log.info(f"Book: {book['title']} ({book['series']} #{book['book_num']})")
    log.info(f"Dir:  {book_dir}")
    log.info(f"Steps: {', '.join(steps)}")
    log.info(f"{'='*60}")
    results = {}
    for step in steps:
        if step not in STEPS:
            log.warning(f"  Unknown step: {step}")
            continue
        if not force and not needs_rebuild(book_key, step, state):
            log.info(f"  [{step}] Skipped (unchanged)")
            results[step] = "skipped"
            continue
        try:
            result = STEPS[step](book_key, book)
            results[step] = result
            mark_built(book_key, step, state)
        except Exception as e:
            log.error(f"  [{step}] FAILED: {e}")
            import traceback
            traceback.print_exc()
            results[step] = f"ERROR: {e}"
    save_state(state)
    return results

def cmd_list():
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print(f"  BOOK PRODUCT LINE — {len(BOOK_REGISTRY)} books across {len(BIBLIOGRAPHY)} series")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    for series_name in BIBLIOGRAPHY:
        books = [(k, b) for k, b in BOOK_REGISTRY.items() if b["series"] == series_name]
        if not books:
            continue
        print(f"\n  {series_name}")
        print(f"  {'-' * (len(series_name) + 2)}")
        for key, book in sorted(books, key=lambda x: x[1]["book_num"]):
            exists = " " if book["dir"].exists() else "!"
            mtype = book["manuscript_type"]
            print(f"    [{exists}] Book {book['book_num']}: {book['title']:<40s} ({mtype})")
    print(f"\n  [!] = directory not found on disk")
    print(f"  Registry keys: {', '.join(sorted(BOOK_REGISTRY.keys()))}")
    print()

def cmd_status():
    state = load_state()
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print(f"  BUILD STATUS")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    for key, book in sorted(BOOK_REGISTRY.items(), key=lambda x: (x[1]["series"], x[1]["book_num"])):
        bs = state.get("books", {}).get(key, {})
        parts = []
        for step in ALL_STEP_NAMES:
            st = bs.get(step, {})
            if st.get("src_hash"):
                built = st.get("built_at", "?")[:10]
                parts.append(f"{step}={built}")
            else:
                parts.append(f"{step}=---")
        print(f"  {book['title']:<40s} {' | '.join(parts)}")
    print()

def cmd_all(series_filter, steps, force):
    books = {k: b for k, b in BOOK_REGISTRY.items()
             if not series_filter or series_filter.lower() in b["series"].lower()}
    log.info(f"Running pipeline for {len(books)} books"
             + (f" (series: {series_filter})" if series_filter else ""))
    summary = {}
    for key in sorted(books, key=lambda k: (books[k]["series"], books[k]["book_num"])):
        summary[key] = run_book(key, steps, force)
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print("SUMMARY")
    print(f"{'='*60}")
    for key, results in summary.items():
        title = BOOK_REGISTRY[key]["title"]
        parts = []
        for step, r in (results or {}).items():
            if r == "skipped":
                parts.append(f"{step}=skip")
            elif isinstance(r, os.PathLike) or (isinstance(r, str) and not r.startswith("ERROR")):
                parts.append(f"{step}=OK")
            elif isinstance(r, str) and r.startswith("ERROR"):
                parts.append(f"{step}=FAIL")
            else:
                parts.append(f"{step}=OK")
        print(f"  {title:<40s} {' | '.join(parts)}")

def cmd_watch(series_filter, steps):
    try:
        from watchdog.observers import Observer
        from watchdog.events import FileSystemEventHandler, FileModifiedEvent
    except ImportError:
        log.error("watchdog not installed. Install with: pip install watchdog")
        sys.exit(1)
    log.info("Starting file-watcher CI/CD mode...")
    log.info(f"Watching: {os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))}")
    log.info("Press Ctrl+C to stop")

    class Handler(FileSystemEventHandler):
        def __init__(self):
            self._debounce = {}
        def on_modified(self, event):
            if event.is_directory:
                return
            p = event.src_path
            if not any(p.endswith(ext) for ext in ('.md', '.xhtml', '.html')):
                return
            if 'manuscript_src' not in p and 'MANUSCRIPT' not in p:
                return
            import time
            now = time.time()
            if now - self._debounce.get(p, 0) < 5:
                return
            self._debounce[p] = now
            for key, book in BOOK_REGISTRY.items():
                if series_filter and series_filter.lower() not in book["series"].lower():
                    continue
                if str(book["dir"]) in p:
                    log.info(f"Change: {p}")
                    log.info(f"Rebuilding: {book['title']}")
                    try:
                        run_book(key, steps, force=True)
                    except Exception as e:
                        log.error(f"Rebuild failed: {e}")
                    break

    handler = Handler()
    observer = Observer()
    watched = set()
    for key, book in BOOK_REGISTRY.items():
        if series_filter and series_filter.lower() not in book["series"].lower():
            continue
        src = book["dir"] / "manuscript_src"
        if src.exists():
            watched.add(str(src))
        watched.add(str(book["dir"]))
    for d in watched:
        observer.schedule(handler, d, recursive=False)
    observer.start()
    log.info(f"Watching {len(watched)} directories. Ctrl+C to stop.")
    import time
    try:
        while True:
            time.sleep(1)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        observer.stop()
        log.info("Watcher stopped.")
    observer.join()

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="hermes-publish: Unified Publishing Pipeline")
    parser.add_argument("--list", action="store_true", help="List all books")
    parser.add_argument("--status", action="store_true", help="Show build status")
    parser.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="Build all books")
    parser.add_argument("--book", type=str, help="Build a specific book (title or key)")
    parser.add_argument("--series", type=str, help="Filter by series name")
    parser.add_argument("--steps", nargs="+", choices=ALL_STEP_NAMES, help="Specific steps to run")
    parser.add_argument("--force", action="store_true", help="Force rebuild even if unchanged")
    parser.add_argument("--watch", action="store_true", help="File-watcher CI/CD mode")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if args.list:
        cmd_list()
    elif args.status:
        cmd_status()
    elif args.watch:
        cmd_watch(args.series, args.steps or ALL_STEP_NAMES)
    elif args.all:
        cmd_all(args.series, args.steps, args.force)
    elif args.book:
        key, _ = find_book(args.book)
        run_book(key, args.steps, args.force)
    else:
        parser.print_help()
        print("\nTip: Use --list to see all books, --status to see build state")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

{"content":""""
MemPalace integration: auto-offload and semantic recall.
Called by the pipeline when memory is full or when cross-session context is needed.
"""
import os, sys, json, logging
from pathlib import Path

log = logging.getLogger("hermes-publish.mempalace")

MEMPALACE_HOME = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/mempalace"))
MEMORY_FILE = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md"))
USER_FILE = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/memories/USER.md"))

def mempalace_available():
    """Check if MemPalace modules are importable."""
    try:
        sys.path.insert(0, str(MEMPALACE_HOME))
        import capture, tag, embed
        return True
    except ImportError:
        return False

def auto_offload(memory_files=None):
    """
    Offload memory entries to MemPalace FAISS vector store.
    Called automatically when MEMORY.md approaches capacity.
    """
    memory_files = memory_files or [MEMORY_FILE, USER_FILE]
    if not mempalace_available():
        log.warning("MemPalace modules not available, skipping offload")
        return False

    sys.path.insert(0, str(MEMPALACE_HOME))
    import capture, tag, embed

    storage_path = str(MEMPALACE_HOME)
    capture.init_capture(storage_path)
    tag.init_tagging(storage_path)
    embed.init_embedding(storage_path)

    from datetime import datetime, timezone
    total = 0

    for mfile in memory_files:
        if not mfile.exists():
            continue
        content = mfile.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        source = "memory" if "MEMORY" in mfile.name else "user_profile"

        # Split on section markers
        entries = content.split("\n§\n") if "§" in content else [content]

        for i, entry in enumerate(entries):
            entry = entry.strip()
            if not entry or len(entry) < 20:
                continue
            try:
                event = {
                    "type": "memory_dump" if source == "memory" else "user_profile",
                    "content": entry,
                    "context": f"auto-offload, {source}",
                    "timestamp": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
                    "source": f"hermes-{source}",
                    "original_index": i,
                }
                event_id = capture.capture_event(event)
                tags = tag.extract_context_tags(entry)
                if tags:
                    tag.save_context_tags(event_id, tags)
                embed.add_embedding(event_id, entry)
                total += 1
            except Exception as e:
                log.error(f"  Offload error: {e}")

    log.info(f"MemPalace offload: {total} entries stored")
    return True

def semantic_recall(query, top_k=5):
    """
    Search MemPalace for relevant context.
    Returns list of (score, content) tuples.
    """
    if not mempalace_available():
        return []

    sys.path.insert(0, str(MEMPALACE_HOME))
    import embed, retrieve

    try:
        results = retrieve.search(query, top_k=top_k)
        return results
    except Exception as e:
        log.error(f"  Recall error: {e}")
        return []

def check_memory_and_offload():
    """
    Check if MEMORY.md is approaching capacity and auto-offload if needed.
    Called at pipeline start.
    """
    if not MEMORY_FILE.exists():
        return

    content = MEMORY_FILE.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    # Hermes MEMORY.md limit is ~2200 chars
    threshold = 1800  # offload proactively at 1800 chars

    if len(content) >= threshold:
        log.info(f"MEMORY.md at {len(content)} chars (threshold: {threshold}), triggering MemPalace offload")
        auto_offload()
        return True
    return False

{"content":""""
Step 7: AI-powered image generation for covers and infographics.
Supports Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (via OpenRouter) and Codex (via OAuth).
"""
import os, sys, json, base64, logging, re
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime

log = logging.getLogger("hermes-publish.images")

def _get_openrouter_key():
    """Get OpenRouter API key from environment or .env files."""
    key = os.environ.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY", "")
    if key:
        return key
    # Try reading from .env files
    for env_path in [
        Path("/mnt/usb_4tb/books/.env"),
        Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/.env")),
        Path(".env"),
    ]:
        if env_path.exists():
            for line in env_path.read_text().splitlines():
                line = line.strip()
                if line.startswith("OPENROUTER_API_KEY="):
                    return line.split("=", 1)[1].strip().strip('"').strip("'")
    return ""

def _get_codex_token():
    """Get Codex OAuth token from environment or .env files."""
    token = os.environ.get("CODEX_OAUTH_TOKEN", "")
    if token:
        return token
    for env_path in [
        Path("/mnt/usb_4tb/books/.env"),
        Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/.env")),
        Path(".env"),
    ]:
        if env_path.exists():
            content = env_path.read_text()
            m = re.search(r'CODEX_OAUTH_TOKEN\s*=\s*(\S+)', content)
            if m:
                return m.group(1).strip().strip('"').strip("'")
    return ""

def generate_image_gemini(prompt, output_path, model="google/gemini-2.5-flash-image"):
    """Generate image using Gemini via OpenRouter."""
    import urllib.request, urllib.error

    api_key = _get_openrouter_key()
    if not api_key:
        log.error("No OPENROUTER_API_KEY found")
        return None

    payload = json.dumps({
        "model": model,
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        "max_tokens": 4096,
    }).encode()

    req = urllib.request.Request(
        "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
        data=payload,
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
            "HTTP-Referer": "https://mifeco.com",
            "X-Title": "Hermes Publish Pipeline",
        },
        method="POST",
    )

    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as resp:
            data = json.loads(resp.read())
    except Exception as e:
        log.error(f"Gemini API error: {e}")
        return None

    try:
        images = data["choices"][0]["message"].get("images", [])
        if not images:
            log.error("No images in response")
            return None
        img_data = images[0]["image_url"]
        # Handle both URL and base64
        if img_data.startswith("data:"):
            b64 = img_data.split(",", 1)[1]
            raw = base64.b64decode(b64)
        elif img_data.startswith("http"):
            with urllib.request.urlopen(img_data, timeout=60) as dl:
                raw = dl.read()
        else:
            raw = base64.b64decode(img_data)
        output_path.write_bytes(raw)
        log.info(f"Image saved: {output_path} ({len(raw)} bytes)")
        return output_path
    except (KeyError, IndexError) as e:
        log.error(f"Failed to parse image response: {e}")
        return None

def generate_image_codex(prompt, output_path):
    """Generate image using Codex CLI (OAuth authenticated)."""
    import subprocess

    token = _get_codex_token()
    if not token:
        log.error("No CODEX_OAUTH_TOKEN found")
        return None

    codex_bin = os.path.expanduser("~/.local/bin/codex")
    if not os.path.exists(codex_bin):

import os, sys, json, logging
from pathlib import Path

log = logging.getLogger("hermes-publish.mempalace")

MEMPALACE_HOME = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/mempalace"))
MEMORY_FILE = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md"))
USER_FILE = Path(os.path.expanduser("~/.hermes/memories/USER.md"))

def mempalace_available():
    """Check if MemPalace modules are importable."""
    if not MEMPALACE_HOME.exists():
        return False
    try:
        sys.path.insert(0, str(MEMPALACE_HOME))
        import capture
        return True
    except ImportError:
        return False

def auto_offload(memory_files=None):
    """
    Offload memory entries to MemPalace FAISS vector store.
    Called automatically when MEMORY.md approaches capacity.
    """
    if not mempalace_available():
        log.warning("MemPalace not available, skipping offload")
        return False

    sys.path.insert(0, str(MEMPALACE_HOME))
    import capture, tag, embed

    sp = str(MEMPALACE_HOME)
    capture.init_capture(sp)
    tag.init_tagging(sp)
    embed.init_embedding(sp)

    memory_files = memory_files or []
    if MEMORY_FILE.exists():
        memory_files.append(MEMORY_FILE)
    if USER_FILE.exists():
        memory_files.append(USER_FILE)

    total = 0
    for mfile in memory_files:
        if not mfile.exists():
            continue
        content = mfile.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        source = "memory" if "MEMORY" in mfile.name else "user_profile"

        # Split on section markers (lines starting with ## or §)
        entries = re.split(r'\n(?=##\s|§\s)', content) if content.strip() else [content]

        for i, entry in enumerate(entries):
            entry = entry.strip()
            if not entry or len(entry) < 20:
                continue
            try:
                event_data = {
                    "content": entry,
                    "context": f"auto-offload, {source}",
                    "source": f"hermes-{source}",
                    "original_index": i,
                }
                event_id = capture.capture_event(event_data)
                if event_id:
                    tags = tag.extract_context_tags(entry)
                    if tags:
                        tag.save_context_tags(event_id, tags)
                    embed.add_embedding(event_id, entry)
                    total += 1
            except Exception as e:
                log.error(f"  Offload error for entry {i}: {e}")

    log.info(f"MemPalace offload: {total} entries stored")
    return True

def semantic_recall(query, top_k=5):
    """Search MemPalace for relevant context."""
    if not mempalace_available():
        return []

    sys.path.insert(0, str(MEMPALACE_HOME))
    import embed, retrieve

    try:
        retrieve.init_retrieval(str(MEMPALACE_HOME))
        results = retrieve.retrieve_memories(query, k=top_k)
        return results
    except Exception as e:

        return auto_offload()
    return False

function.arguments:
{"content":"#!/bin/bash
# hermes-publish-watcher: File-watcher CI/CD for the book publishing pipeline
# Starts the watchdog that auto-rebuilds books when manuscript files change.
#
# Usage:
#   ./hermes-publish-watcher start    # start the watcher
#   ./hermes-publish-watcher stop     # stop the watcher
#   ./hermes-publish-watcher status   # check if running
#   ./hermes-publish-watcher restart  # restart

PIDFILE="/tmp/hermes-publish-watcher.pid"
LOGFILE="/tmp/hermes-publish-watcher.log"
PIPELINE="/mnt/usb_4tb/books/hermes_publish.py"

start() {
    if [ -f "$PIDFILE" ] && kill -0 "$(cat $PIDFILE)" 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "Watcher already running (PID $(cat $PIDFILE))"
        return
    fi
    echo "Starting hermes-publish file-watcher..."
    nohup python3 "$PIPELINE" --watch > "$LOGFILE" 2>&1 &
    echo $! > "$PIDFILE"
    echo "Started (PID $!, log: $LOGFILE)"
}

stop() {
    if [ -f "$PIDFILE" ]; then
        PID=$(cat "$PIDFILE")
        if kill -0 "$PID" 2>/dev/null; then
            kill "$PID"
            rm -f "$PIDFILE"
            echo "Stopped (PID $PID)"
        else
            echo "Not running (stale PID file)"
            rm -f "$PIDFILE"
        fi
    else
        echo "Not running"
    fi
}

status() {
    if [ -f "$PIDFILE" ] && kill -0 "$(cat $PIDFILE)" 2>/dev/null; then
        echo "Running (PID $(cat $PIDFILE))"
        echo "Log: $LOGFILE"
    else
        echo "Not running"
        rm -f "$PIDFILE" 2>/dev/null
    fi
}

case "${1:-status}" in
    start)  start ;;
    stop)   stop ;;
    restart) stop; sleep 1; start ;;
    status) status ;;
    *)      echo "Usage: $0 {start|stop|restart|status}" ;;
esac

## Part I: Opening Arguments (Chapters 1-8) — Setup

### Chapter 1 — The Letterhead Lies
- **Beat 1:** Cindy Lou opens her solo practice in a tiny office above a laundromat. Printer jams on her first business card run. The dead plant in the corner was dead when she moved in. She has $847 in her business account and a recurring DreamSoda habit.
- **Beat 2:** She attends a junior lawyers' networking mixer at a Midtown wine bar. She spills rosé on her only good blazer and overhears two associates laughing about solo practitioners who "hang a shingle before they can afford shoelaces." She introduces herself anyway—too fast, too loud, too eager.
- **Beat 3:** Walking home through Tompkins Square Park, Cindy strides past a woman crying on a bench. The woman is Emma Johnson. Cindy almost keeps walking. Turns around. Emma has a lease dispute—her landlord is trying to evict her over a bogus "aroma nuisance" clause. Cindy takes the case on the spot. First client. Zero retainer. End with Cindy texting Ira: "I have a client. Send help."

### Chapter 2 — The Aroma of Doom
- **Beat 1:** Cindy visits Emma's bakery, "Sugar Rush," in a rapidly gentrifying block in the East Village. The bakery is everything Cindy's practice is not—popular, established, fragrant. Emma explains the dispute: landlord Marcus Webb claims her baking violates a clause about "noxious odors" and "commercial aroma displacement."
- **Beat 2:** Cindy researches the clause and finds it's almost unenforceable—but the lease language is weirdly specific. She files it under "things I don't have time to investigate."
- **Beat 3:** Cindy submits a motion to dismiss. It's good work—clean, thorough, possibly the best thing she's ever written. She emails it at 3 AM, then lies awake wondering if she even filed in the right court.

### Chapter 3 — The Poodle Principle
- **Beat 1:** Liam Carter arrives at Cindy's office—windblown, anxious, smelling like dog shampoo. He's a dog walker accused of losing Mrs. Whitfield's prize poodle, "Reginald the Third." {"output": "=== BOOK 1 CHAPTER 1 ===
The Letterhead Lies

    The printer jammed on the forty-third business card, which felt about right. I'd been feeding sheets into the thing for twenty minutes—good card stock, cream-colored, the kind that whispered *serious professional* instead of *desperate recent graduate*—and every third or fourth pass, the machine made a sound like a small animal dying and then swallowed the paper whole. I knelt beside it, popped the access panel, and found the card curled inside like a tiny scroll of failure. The ink had smeared across Cindy Lou Walsh, Attorney at Law in a Rorschach blot that looked disturbingly like a noose.

    I peeled the ruined card free, dropped it on the pile of forty-two predecessors, and stared at the dead plant in the corner. It had been dead when I signed the lease. The previous tenant—a tax preparer named Gerald who'd fled to New Jersey under circumstances the landlord described as "complicated"—had left behind a potted fern so desiccated it crumbled if you looked at it too hard. I'd meant to throw it out. That was three weeks ago. Now it was a monument. A dry, brown, slightly judgmental monument to every decision that had led me to this office above a laundromat on East 7th Street, where the floor vibrated every time someone ran a spin cycle and the air permanently smelled like lavender detergent and surrender.

    My business account held eight hundred and forty-seven dollars. I knew this because I'd checked it that morning, and the morning before, and the morning before that, watching the number with the same obsessive attention I used to give my law school outlines—color-coded, cross-referenced, annotated in margins so small you needed a magnifying glass. The difference was that my outlines had gotten me a J.D. This number was going to get me evicted.

    I had a recurring DreamSoda habit that cost me eleven dollars a week, which meant I could sustain my preferred method of caffeine delivery for roughly seventy-seven weeks before I'd have to switch to coffee like some kind of animal. This was the kind of math I did now. Not torts. Not contracts. Soda budgets.

    I fed another sheet into the printer. It went through clean. I watched the card emerge—my name, my phone number, my email, the little scales of justice I'd designed myself in a free vector program at two in the morning. They looked almost real. Almost like they belonged to a person who had her life arranged in an order that made sense.

    The card came out perfect. I set it on my desk—a folding table I'd bought at a church supply store because it was the only surface I could afford that didn't wobble—and allowed myself exactly five seconds of pride. Then the printer jammed again.

---

    The networking mixer was at a wine bar in Midtown called something I immediately forgot, the way you forget the name of a medication you don't want to need. It was the kind of place where the lighting was designed to make everyone look like they'd just returned from somewhere expensive, and the menus didn't list prices because if you had to ask, you were in the wrong room. I was definitely in the wrong room. But the Junior Bar Association had sent the invitation to every newly admitted attorney in the five boroughs, and I'd RSVP'd before I could talk myself out of it, which was the only way I ever did anything brave.

    I wore my only good blazer—navy, single-breasted, bought on sale at a store that had since gone out of business, which felt symbolic in a way I didn't want to examine. Under it, a white blouse I'd ironed twice. I'd taken the subway and walked the last four blocks because the office was in the Village and Midtown was Midtown and some distances you just had to cover on foot, in heels, pretending you belonged.

    The room was full of lawyers. I don't know what I expected—maybe a few nervous solo practitioners like me, huddled near the shrimp, trading war stories about printer jams and dead ferns. Instead, it was associates from firms I'd applied to and been rejected by, wearing suits that fit like they'd been grown on their bodies, holding wine glasses with the casual confidence of people who understood that the glass was supposed to be held by the stem and not clutched like a lifeline. I clutched like a lifeline.

    A server passed with a tray of rosé. I took one because holding something gave my hands a job, and because rosé felt like the kind of wine that wouldn't judge me for not knowing anything about wine. I was wrong about that too. The second I lifted the glass, I caught my heel on the edge of someone's bag—a leather bag, expensive, the kind that costs more than my rent—and the rosé left the glass in a graceful arc that ended on the front of my blazer.

    Navy fabric, white wine. The stain bloomed like a rose opening in time-lapse, right over my left breast, as if my body were trying to grow a flower to commemorate the occasion.

    "Oh God," I said, too loud. "Oh no. Oh—sorry, I'm so—does anyone have—"

    A woman in a charcoal suit handed me a cocktail napkin. I dabbed at the stain, which only spread it, which only made me dab harder, which only made the woman in the charcoal suit take a step back, as if clumsiness were contagious.

    I gave up. I held the napkin against the stain like a field medic applying pressure to a wound and scanned the room for the exit. That's when I heard them—two men, mid-thirties, standing near the bar with the easy posture of people who'd never had wine on their only good blazer.

    "—saw another one today," the taller one was saying. "Solo practitioner. Opened shop above a laundromat, if you can believe it."

    The shorter one laughed. "They're hanging a shingle before they can afford shoelaces. It's actually kind of sad."

    "It's actually kind of hilarious. Give it six months. They'll be back on the market, begging for document review gigs."

    I was standing close enough that they could see me. Close enough that the stain on my blazer was visible, and the napkin, and the way my jaw had gone tight in the way that meant I was about to do something I'd either regret or be proud of, with no middle ground.

    I walked over. Fast. Too fast. I was always too fast—too fast with my words, too fast with my walking, too fast with my decisions. Ira Mason said I moved through life like a closing argument that skipped the evidence and went straight to the verdict.

    "Hi," I said. "Cindy Lou Walsh. I'm a solo practitioner. Above a laundromat, actually. You were just talking about me, I think—or someone like me, which is almost worse because it means you've got a whole category, a whole taxonomy of people you've decided are jokes before you've met them, and I just want to say that I have a J.D. from a school you've heard of, and I passed the bar on my first try, and my office smells like lavender detergent, which is honestly not the worst thing in the world, and I'm going to be a very good lawyer, and I'm sorry about the wine, and I'm sorry if I'm talking too fast, I know I'm talking too fast, but I just—"

    I stopped. The two men stared at me. The taller one's mouth was open. The shorter one's wine glass was frozen halfway to his lips.

    "—I'm going to go now," I said.

    I went.

    In the bathroom, I looked at myself in the mirror. The stain had dried to a pale pink shadow. My hair had started to escape the clip I'd put it in. My eyes had the bright, slightly unhinged look they got when I'd said too much, which was most of the time. I pressed my palms against the cool edge of the sink and breathed.

    I did not cry. Cindy Lou Walsh, Attorney at Law, did not cry in the bathroom of a Midtown wine bar. She fixed her hair, blotted the stain one more time, and went back out to shake hands and hand out business cards and pretend that the last five minutes hadn't happened.

    I stayed for another forty minutes. I talked to a public defender named Marco who had kind eyes and a caseload that would kill a normal person. I talked to a woman who did immigration law from her kitchen table in Queens. I handed out six business cards. Nobody laughed at me to my face, which I counted as a win.

    On my way out, I passed the two men by the bar. The shorter one raised his glass in a little salute. I gave him a nod that I hoped communicated *I see you and I'm going to forget you* and pushed through the door into the cold.

# Chapter 15: The Dog Collar Redemption

The email from SafePup Industries arrived at 6:47 AM on a Thursday, thirteen minutes before my alarm went off, which was the universe's way of telling me that the night shift at a GPS collar company in Paramus, New Jersey, operated on a schedule that recognized no mercy.

I read it in bed, Dolly purring on my chest like a small furry engine of indifference. The email was from a man named Gerald Voight, SafePup's head of data compliance, and it was the kind of corporate communication that took three paragraphs to say something that should have taken three sentences: we have your data, we verified the release form, here are the files.

Thirty days of Reginald's GPS data. Every five-minute ping when he was moving. Every thirty-minute stationary marker when he was not. Encrypted, timestamped, and uploaded automatically to SafePup's cloud servers at the end of each day. Gerald Voight's email included a fifteen-page technical appendix explaining the data format and a cover note that managed to be simultaneously thorough and completely useless to anyone who didn't speak server architecture.

I didn't speak server architecture. But I knew someone who did.

Ted picked up on the second ring. He sounded awake, which meant he'd been up for at least an hour already, because Ted rose at five every morning with the punctuality of a man who'd been military and had never seen a reason to stop. "Tell me something good," he said.

"SafePup came through. Thirty days of Reginald's GPS data. The files are on my email. I need you to make them make sense."

"I'll be at your office in forty minutes."

He made it in thirty-five. I know because I checked the clock the way I always checked the clock when waiting for something that mattered—obsessively, like time was a witness I was trying to keep on the stand. Ted came through the door with his laptop bag and the particular energy of a man who'd just been handed a puzzle and was already inside it.

I made coffee. Not good coffee—the machine in my office had been broken for two weeks and I'd been using a pour-over setup that produced something in the neighborhood of what coffee would be if coffee had given up on its aspirations. Ted drank it without complaint, which was how I knew he was focused. Complaining about my coffee was one of Ted's few recreational activities, and when he didn't do it, he was working.

He opened the SafePup files and started working through the data. I watched him work the way I'd learned to watch Ted work: quietly, from a distance, without asking questions that would slow him down. His face did the things it did—the eyebrow lip press, the occasional murmur when something caught his attention. I drank my terrible coffee and waited.

Twenty minutes later, he said, "Liam."

I set down my cup. "Liam."

"Liam was the one walking Reginald during the key dates. Not Emma. Not Angela the dog walker. Liam. Every Tuesday and Friday for four weeks straight, the data shows a consistent walking pattern: start at Emma's building on West 82nd, head south on Broadway, hit the midtown corridor, loop back. The route takes between forty-five minutes and two hours, depending on the day."

"Do the days line up with the fraud activity?"

Ted turned the laptop toward me. On the screen was a map of Manhattan—Google Maps, overlaid with blue dots connected by thin lines. Each line was a walk. Each dot was a pause. The lines converged on four locations, marked with red pins.

"This one," Ted said, pointing to a red pin on West 47th Street, "is the Bennett Foundation's processing center. The converted warehouse. Reginald was here on October 9th, October 16th, and October 23rd. Three Tuesdays. Each time for approximately twelve minutes."

The dates hit me like a door opening. October 9th was the Evergreen Outreach account opening. October 16th was the second shell deposit. October 23rd was the Meridian Services Group transfer. Three trades. Three Tuesdays. Three visits from a white poodle who had no idea he was leaving a trail.

"This one," Ted continued, moving the cursor to a second red pin, "is the Marcus Webb Management Company. West 52nd Street, third floor of a commercial building, suite 304. According to the filings I pulled last week, Webb is the registered agent for seven entities connected to the Bennett Foundation's grant network. Reginald was here on October 13th, October 27th, and November 3rd. Three Fridays."

Marcus Webb. The name I'd been chasing through corporate filings for three weeks—the shell company architect, the man whose signature appeared on documents I'd never been able to connect to anyone with a face. Ted's surveillance photos had given me a face: mid-fifties, the kind of expensive blandness that made you forget him the moment he left the room, except Ted never forgot anyone and his photos were crystalline. Now Reginald had given me something better than a face. He'd given me a timestamp.

# Chapter 30: Retainer to Trouble

    The plant named Objection had three new leaves by the time the one-year anniversary rolled around, which felt like some kind of omen. Plants don't know what anniversaries are. They just grow or they don't, and the ones that don't end up brown and crumbly in the corner of your office like a rebuke from God. But Objection — the successor to the dead fern Gerald the tax preparer had left behind, and the successor to the pathos I'd nearly killed in my first year — Objection had not only survived, it had *thrived*. Three new leaves, bright green and waxy, unfurling from the center like tiny hands reaching for something they couldn't see.

    I watered it on a Wednesday morning in late December, three months after the verdict, and watched the water soil and thought about everything that had brought me to this point: a larger desk, a working printer, a wall of color-coded files, and a plant with a legal name that made Priya smile every time she said it.

    My practice had twelve active cases. Twelve. I said the number out loud sometimes, just to feel it, the way you repeat a word until it stops sounding like a word and starts sounding like what it means. Twelve meant the referral chain was still running. Twelve meant the neighborhood had decided I was real. Twelve meant that somewhere in the city, twelve people were dealing with the particular helplessness of having a legal problem and not knowing what to do about it, and they'd called my number, which was listed on a website Priya had built using a template and an attention to detail that bordered on architecture.

    Priya Sharma had started as my first part-time assistant and was now my second part-time assistant, because I'd hired a second part-time assistant. Her name was Marcus Webb — no relation to the Webb who'd testified in the Brady matter, though he'd made the joke himself during his interview, which was how I knew he had the right temperament for this work. Marcus was twenty-six, had spent two years at a mid-sized firm doing document review, and had quit because, in his words, "I wanted to help actual people instead of redacting the same privileged email for the ninth hundredth time." He worked Tuesdays and Thursdays. Priya worked Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. They overlapped on Wednesdays, which was when we had our case review meetings, which were exactly as exciting as they sounded and absolutely essential.

    The office had grown, too. Not much — I wasn't moving to Midtown, wasn't renting a suite with frosted glass doors and a receptionist named Blythe — but the laundromat owner downstairs, Mrs. Pham, had renovated both locations, and the new space was what I would generously call "upgraded." The floor no longer vibrated during the spin cycle. The smell had shifted from "lavender detergent and surrender" to "lavender detergent and mild optimism." There was a proper door with a real lock — not the deadbolt that had gotten shattered during the break-in, but a deadbolt reinforced with a steel strike plate that Ted had installed on a Saturday morning while wearing a tool belt and an expression of extreme purpose.

    I still worked above a laundromat. I'd made my peace with it. The bounce in the floor had been replaced by a kind of gentle hum, like a building that was alive and content, and some mornings I'd sit at my desk and hear the machines below and feel, absurdly, like the building was breathing with me.

    The anniversary party was Emma's idea.

    She called me on a Tuesday — not Priya's Tuesday, my Tuesday, which meant Emma had my personal number, which she'd gotten from Sophia, who'd gotten it from Liam, who'd gotten it from me on the night of my third case, when I'd been sitting on the courthouse steps and needed a lawyer I didn't have yet. That was how the neighborhood worked. Information flowed like water through the cracks, finding the lowest point, filling every gap.

    "One year," Emma said. "Since you opened. We're doing this."

    "We're doing what?"

    "A party. Sugar Rush. Saturday evening. I'm making a cake. Liam's got the decorations. Sophia's pulling together the food—"

    "Emma, I don't need a—"

    "Shut up, Cindy. It's not optional. Six o'clock."

    She hung up. I looked at my phone. I looked at Objection, whose new leaves seemed to be leaning slightly in my direction, as if to say, *Go to the party.*

    I went to the party.

    Sugar Rush looked different at night. During the day, it was all natural light and apron strings and the smell of sugar and yeast. At night — at six on a Saturday in December, with the streetlights on and the windows fogged from the inside — it looked like something out of a story. Emma had strung small white lights along the ceiling. Liam had taped paper signs to the walls that read "HAPPY ANNIVERSARY CINDY" in his careful, architectural-precision handwriting. Sophia had arranged a table of food that was either a spread or a small feast, depending on your threshold for abundance: empanadas, plantains, rice and beans, a tray of Emma's cinnamon rolls that was less a food item and more a public service.

    The cake was two layers, chocolate, with white frosting and the words "ONE YEAR OF TROUBLE" written across the top in Emma's looping cursive. I saw it and felt something crack open in my chest, the way a shell cracks — not breaking, but opening to whatever was inside.

    "You spelled 'trouble' right," I said.

    "I always spell 'trouble' right. Trouble is my first language."", "exit_code": 0, "error": null}

    The printer jammed on the forty-third business card, which felt about right.     I fed another sheet through. The card emerged perfect—my name, my phone number, my homemade scales of justice. I allowed myself five seconds of pride. Then the printer jammed again.

---

    The Junior Bar Association mixer was at a Midtown wine bar where the lighting was designed to make everyone look imported from somewhere expensive. I wore my only good blazer—navy, bought on sale at a store that had since gone out of business, which felt symbolic.

    Associates from firms that had rejected me filled the room, wearing suits that fit like they'd been grown on their bodies. I clutched my rosé by the stem.     Nearby, two men talked. "Solo practitioner. Opened shop above a laundromat." The shorter one laughed. "Hanging a shingle before they can afford shoelaces."

    I walked over. Too fast. I was always too fast. "Hi. Cindy Lou Walsh. Solo practitioner. Above a laundromat, actually. You were just talking about me—or someone like me, which is worse, because it means you've got a whole taxonomy—"

    I stopped. They stared. "I'm going to go now," I said.

    I stayed forty minutes. Handed out six business cards. Nobody laughed to my face.

---

    I walked home through Tompkins Square Park. A woman sat on a bench near the dog run, crying. I almost kept walking. I had enough problems.

    I turned around.

    "Hi. I'm Cindy Lou. I'm a lawyer. Are you okay?"

    She studied me. "You just started? And you're offering to help for free?"

    I hadn't thought about the money part. "We can figure that out later. First, I need to see your lease."

    Her name was Emma Johnson. Twelve years in the same building. New landlord, Marcus Webb, had bought it eight months ago and had been looking for reasons to empty it ever since.

{"content":"Discovery and Disaster

    The courthouse at eight AM was a living system—lawyers, litigants, clerks flowing through revolving doors with the grim efficiency of blood cells through a vein. I was there for Noah Martinez's pre-trial conference, dreading it. Not because I didn't want a deal, but because I wasn't ready. I had questions without answers and my own address on a fraudulent filing.

    ADA Ethan Moore waited in Conference Room 4C—a repurposed storage closet with delusions of grandeur. Early thirties, off-the-rack suit, handshake calibrated like a negotiation before the negotiation.

    He slid a page across the table. "Plea offer. One count attempted wire fraud, Class A misdemeanor. No jail time. Three years' probation, full restitution."

    I read it twice. "No jail time for a case your office spent six days building."

    "The evidence is solid. Signatures, bank records, cooperating witnesses. Mr. Martinez is a first-time offender. We're being generous."

    *Generous.* The word prosecutors used when they wanted you to feel grateful.

    "I need forty-eight hours."

    "To do what?"

    "To investigate. To review discovery. To advise my client based on something other than the assurance that you're being generous."

    Moore leaned back. "This case isn't complicated. Your client signed the forms. The money moved. I'd encourage you not to make this harder than it is."

    "I'll take forty-eight hours."

    He studied me. "You have until Thursday morning. Then the offer expires and we proceed to trial." He paused at the door. "I mean it about not making this harder than it is."

    I sat alone in the storage closet and thought about how easy it would be to take the deal. But my address was on a fraudulent filing, M. Webb's signature moved two hundred thousand dollars, and none of it was simple.

---

    In the courthouse clerk's office, a woman with tilted glasses and an oatmeal cardigan stopped me. "Harper Davis, court clerk. I processed your notice of appearance for Noah Martinez." She typed rapidly, pulling up the corporate filings database. "Three shell companies in the indictment. Look at the registered agent addresses."

    Evergreen Outreach: a retired postal worker in Flushing who'd never heard of them. The Bennett Foundation: a co-working space in Brooklyn. Helping Hands Collective: my address. Above the laundromat. Suite 2B.

    "Someone's using new lawyers as mail drops," Harper said. "New solos print their addresses on everything—bar registration, letterhead, business cards. Easy to find, easy to exploit. Low profile, no compliance department."

    Three addresses. Three entities. Three people who didn't know.

    "Could you look up who incorporated these entities?" I asked.

    "Give me an hour."

    Forty minutes later she handed me a printout with three names circled in red. The incorporator of the Bennett Foundation was Marcus Webb. Emma's landlord. The machinery behind the aroma nuisance case was the same machinery behind Noah's fraud charges.

---

    Ira's apartment in Washington Heights smelled like instant ramen and isopropyl alcohol—forensic chemist meets college student, neither of which ever cleaned. He answered on the third ring. "Cindy. It's late. Are you dead?"

    "Not yet. I'm outside your building. I brought dumplings."

    The buzzer sounded before I finished the sentence.

    Ira examined the authorization forms under his magnifying lamp, nitrile gloves on, the way a surgeon prepares. "Forged signatures reveal themselves through boring details. Pen pressure. Stroke speed. Where the ink pools. Whether the writer lifted the pen where they should have."

    He set the forms down. "These are photocopies—I can't confirm forgery from these. But the signature on the Bennett Foundation form has heavier downstrokes than the Evergreen form. Either the forger was inconsistent, or two different people made these."

    He pulled up Noah's driver's license scan. "Look at the 'N' in Noah. On his license, the first stroke starts above the baseline—a specific habit. On the forms, it starts at the baseline. Small difference. Most people wouldn't notice."

    "That's not proof," Ira said, because Ira always said that. "It's an indicator."

    I told him everything. Harper's discovery. The printout. Marcus Webb's name connecting everything—the shell companies, the property holdings, my address on a filing I'd never signed.

    Ira reached across his desk, stuck a Post-it to the leftover dumplings: NOT EVIDENCE. Then he looked at me with the expression reserved for when the data had exceeded the model.

    "You need to be careful. This isn't a poodle case. This isn't a bakery lease. If the same person is behind all of this, you're inside the thing. And people who build structures like this don't appreciate it when someone pulls at the threads."

    I looked at the printout. Marcus Webb's name sat on the page like a door I'd been walking past for weeks without realizing it was open.

    "I have until Thursday morning," I said.

    I ate a cold dumpling. Outside, the city hummed its low constant hum, and somewhere in it Marcus Webb was building empires out of other people's names. I pulled out my phone and called Sophia. "I found something. I need you to find out everything about Marcus Webb."

"""
Condense a chapter by keeping key narrative elements and cutting ~55% of words.
Strategy:
1. Keep chapter title
2. For each paragraph: if it's dialogue, keep it. If it's plot-critical, keep ~50%. If it's description/atmosphere, keep ~30%.
3. Keep scene breaks (---) and humor beats
4. Keep the first and last 2 sentences of each chapter intact
"""
import re

def condense_chapter(content, target_ratio=0.45):
    lines = content.split('\n')
    
    # Extract chapter title (first line)
    title = lines[0] if lines else ""
    
    # Split into paragraphs (separated by blank lines)
    paragraphs = []
    current = []
    for line in lines[1:]:
        stripped = line.strip()
        if not stripped:
            if current:
                paragraphs.append('\n'.join(current))
                current = []
        else:
            current.append(line)
    if current:
        paragraphs.append('\n'.join(current))
    
    # Process paragraphs
    result = [title, ""]
    
    for i, para in enumerate(paragraphs):
        # Always keep scene breaks
        if para.strip() == '---' or para.strip() == '* * *':
            result.append("")
            result.append("---")
            result.append("")
            continue
        
        # Skip empty
        if not para.strip():
            continue
        
        # Determine paragraph type
        text = para.strip()
        
        # Dialogue-heavy paragraphs: keep more
        quote_count = text.count('"')
        is_dialogue = quote_count >= 2
        
        # Plot-critical (contains key names/evidence): keep more
        key_terms = ['Moore', 'Webb', 'Noah', 'Olivia', 'Bennett', 'evidence', 'signature', 
                     'filing', 'fraud', 'GPS', 'collar', 'hearing', 'arrest', 'deal',
                     'plea', 'shell', 'foundation', 'arrested', 'court', 'judge', 'Bill',
                     'Ted', 'Ira', 'Emma', 'Liam', 'Sophia']
        is_critical = sum(1 for t in key_terms if t in text) >= 2
        
        # First/last paragraph: keep more
        if i < 3 or i > len(paragraphs) - 3:
            keep_ratio = 0.75
        elif is_dialogue:
            keep_ratio = 0.70
        elif is_critical:
            keep_ratio = 0.50
        elif len(text.split()) < 30:
            keep_ratio = 0.60  # short paragraphs: keep most
        else:
            keep_ratio = 0.35  # long descriptive: keep less
        
        # Apply compression by keeping selected sentences
        sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text)
        if not sentences:
            continue
        
        # For long paragraphs, keep every Nth sentence based on ratio
        if len(sentences) > 3:
            n = max(2, int(1 / keep_ratio))
            kept = []
            for j, s in enumerate(sentences):
                # Always keep first sentence of paragraph
                if j == 0:
                    kept.append(s)
                # Keep sentences with dialogue
                elif '"' in s:
                    kept.append(s)
                # Keep every Nth sentence
                elif j % n == 0:
                    kept.append(s)
                # Keep short punchy sentences
                elif len(s.split()) < 15 and j > 0:
                    kept.append(s)
            
            # Reconstruct with proper indentation
            compressed = ' '.join(kept)
        else:
            compressed = text
        
        result.append("")
        result.append(compressed)
    
    return '\n'.join(result)

She'd built a machine that moved money from a legitimate financial advisory firm into her own charity, layered it through three shell entities, and converted it into real estate—buildings she could fill with tenants she could evict when the rent numbers stopped making sense. Emma's bakery wasn't a target because of Marcus Webb's greed. It was a target because the building was a hole that needed filling, and the foundation's money needed somewhere clean to land.
     8|
     9|    Sophia's bank statements had shown $203,000 in fraudulent transfers. But that was just the Graham & Sundheim money. The Bennett Foundation's own books—the ones I'd photographed with cocktail sauce on my hands and a security guard closing in—showed another $2.1 million in "program expenses" to entities that didn't exist, spread over fourteen months. It was $2.3 million, Noah Martinez's transfers were the visible tip, and my office had been chosen as a registered agent because I was new and small and nobody.

Emma's landlord wasn't a landlord. He was a node. The holding company wasn't a holding company. It was a pipe. And the Bennett Foundation wasn't a charity. {"content":"The Romantic Tease

    Bill made a reservation at a place on the Upper West Side that had cloth napkins. I knew they were cloth because I picked one up to wipe coffee off my sleeve and it was so clearly, aggressively cloth that using it for anything so mundane felt like a crime against textiles.

    Everyone knew Bill's name—the hostess, the sommelier, the waiter who brought the amuse-bouche. Being invited into Bill's life was either a privilege or a warning.

    "You're staring at the menu," he said.

    The menus didn't list prices. I'd learned to hate that particular luxury.

    "You did the thing," Bill said, leaning in. "The thing where you calculate whether the risotto costs more than your car payment. I can see it in your face."

    I deflected with humor—my default setting. Bill laughed. The waiter brought wine that probably cost more than my first month's rent. We talked about the case, about the aftermath, about what comes after the verdict when the adrenaline fades and you're just a person again, sitting in a nice restaurant, trying to remember which fork to use.

    "I'm glad you're not dead," Bill said, at one point, quite seriously.

    "I'm glad I'm not dead too."

    It was a good dinner. Bill walked me home. At my laundromat entrance, he kissed my cheek—briefly, lightly, a punctuation mark. "Good night, Cindy Lou."

    I went upstairs, changed into pajamas, and found a text from Ted: *Nice dinner?*

    *How did you know about dinner?*

    *Your office light was on at 10. Bill's car service doesn't come to the East Village unless you're going somewhere nice. Plus Ira told me.*

    *Ira has a big mouth for a forensic analyst.*

    *Text me tomorrow. I want to hear about the fork situation.*

    I smiled in the dark. My romantic docket was a disaster. But my cases were closed, my clients were free, and I had two people who cared enough to check on me. That was enough.

{"content":"The Closing Argument

    I didn't need to write a closing argument. The trial was over, the jury had spoken, Noah was free. But on a Thursday morning, three weeks after the verdict, I sat at my desk with a legal pad and a pen that didn't skip (a gift from Bill) and I wrote it anyway.

    Not for the court. Not for the grievance committee or the FBI or the blogger from West Side Legal who'd been emailing me twice a week. I wrote it for me. Because if I was going to be a lawyer—a real lawyer, with a real office and real cases—I needed to understand what I'd actually learned.

    Here's what I wrote: A frame job is only as strong as the frame. Pick at the edges and the whole picture falls apart. Forgers get the shape right but the rhythm wrong—bad jazz. A poodle with a GPS collar is worth more than a thousand affidavits. The dead plant in the corner of your office is a metaphor for what happens when you stop paying attention. And the best evidence doesn't come from a courtroom—it comes from a bike messenger, a forensic analyst who labels his dumplings, and a crying woman on a bench in Tompkins Square Park.

    I wrote for an hour. Then I put the legal pad in my desk drawer, next to forty-three business cards with Rorschach blots where my name should have been, and I went back to work.

    My practice had grown. Not much—I wasn't moving to Midtown—but the referral chain was running. Denise Okafor had referred a friend. That friend had referred someone else. The neighborhood had decided I was real.

    My phone buzzed. A new client. A tenant dispute. Nothing dramatic. Nothing that would end up on the news.

    I took the case. Of course I did. I was Cindy Lou Walsh, Attorney at Law. Above a laundromat.

    And I was just getting started.

    Denise Okafor arrived at two o'clock on the dot, which told me more about her than the intake form ever would. People who've been wronged and still show up on time are people who believe the system works. I used to be one of those people.
