    "Ms. Walsh. Thank you for seeing me on short notice."

    "Of course. What's the situation?"

    She laid it out cleanly—a landlord dispute, a lease violation claim, a building that had changed ownership six months ago. She'd been there twelve years. The new owner wanted her out. The reasons kept changing: noise complaints, unauthorized guests, a clause about "building harmony" that sounded made up.

    It didn't sound made up. It sounded like Marcus Webb's "aroma nuisance" clause. Different building, different landlord, same playbook.

    "I'll need to see your lease," I said. "And any correspondence from the new management company."

    She handed me a folder. Thick, organized, color-coded. I opened it and felt the particular thrill I got when a client had done their homework.

    "I'll review this and get back to you within 48 hours," I said. "In the meantime, don't sign anything they send you."

    She nodded. Stood. Shook my hand with a grip that was firm but not aggressive. "I heard about the Martinez case. That's why I called you."

    After she left, I spread the documents across my desk. Same shell company structure. Same pattern of harassment. Different borough, same playbook.

    I picked up my phone and called Ethan Moore. "I think there might be more buildings. More tenants. The same pattern."

{"content":"The Printer's Revenge

    The printer was new. That was the problem with new things—they hadn't yet learned their place.

    I'd bought it three weeks ago, a sleek black thing with wireless capability and the implicit promise that this time, finally, the technology would behave. It had been behaving. It had printed the Denise Okafor filing without complaint. It had handled fourteen drafts of my YLNY speech. It had even survived Ira's forty-page forensic report, which he'd sent at 11 PM with a note: "Page 23 has a typo. Don't read page 23."

    The printer had handled all of this with the quiet competence of a machine that understood its role.

    Then it jammed. On the most important document of the week. A motion to compel discovery in the Denise Okafor case, due in court at nine AM, and the printer ate it with the same sound it had made forty-three times before I'd replaced it: a small animal dying.

    I knelt beside it. Popped the access panel. Found the card curled inside like a tiny scroll of failure.

    The ink had smeared across "Cindy Lou Walsh, Attorney at Law" in a Rorschach blot that looked disturbingly like a noose.

    I laughed. Because what else do you do? The printer had declared war on me again, and I'd been here before, and I'd survive it again.

    I walked six blocks to Kinko's. The machine worked. Every page. No jams.

    Some things, at least, were reliable.
","path":"/mnt/usb_4tb/books/Cindy_Lou_Legal_Capers/cindy-lou-series/book-1-retainer-to-trouble/chapters/ch28.md"}

{"content":"Retainer to Trouble

    The plant named Objection had three new leaves by the time the one-year anniversary rolled around. Plants don't know what anniversaries are. They just grow or they don't. But Objection—successor to the dead fern Gerald the tax preparer had left behind—had not only survived, it had thrived. Three new leaves, bright green and waxy, unfurling from the center like tiny hands reaching for something they couldn't see.

    I watered it on a Wednesday morning in late December, three months after the verdict, and thought about everything that had brought me here: a larger desk, a working printer, a wall of files, and a plant with a legal name that made Priya smile every time she said it.

    My practice had twelve active cases. Twelve. I said the number out loud sometimes, just to feel it. Twelve meant the referral chain was running. Twelve meant the neighborhood had decided I was real.

    The anniversary party was Emma's idea. Sugar Rush, Saturday evening. I arrived at six to find the bakery transformed—white lights along the ceiling, paper signs reading "HAPPY ANNIVERSARY CINDY" in Liam's architectural-precision handwriting, a table of food that was either a spread or a small feast.

    The cake was two layers, chocolate, with white frosting and the words "ONE YEAR OF TROUBLE" written across the top in Emma's looping cursive. I saw it and felt something crack open in my chest—not breaking, but opening to whatever was inside.

    "You spelled 'trouble' right," I said.

    "I always spell 'trouble' right. Trouble is my first language."

    I looked around the room. Emma, who'd been crying on a bench when I met her. Liam, who'd brought me a missing poodle and a bike messenger. Sophia, whose brother was home because I'd refused to take the deal. Ira, in a suit that still didn't quite fit, eating a cinnamon roll with the focused intensity of a man analyzing pastry grain. Bill, who'd brought croissants and financial forensics and a kiss on the cheek. Ted, who'd brought a GPS collar and a bike and the kind of loyalty that doesn't come with a retainer agreement.

    My people. The ones who'd trusted me when I was just a woman with a secondhand desk and a bar card and a photocopier that jammed if you looked at it wrong.

    I picked up my fork. I looked at the cake. I looked at Objection's photo on my phone—the plant I'd brought home from the office, thriving on my windowsill.

    "Thank you," I said, to everyone, to no one, to the city that had tried to swallow me and had, instead, coughed me back up.

    I was Cindy Lou Walsh, Attorney at Law. I worked above a laundromat. I had a recurring DreamSoda habit and a plant with a legal name and twelve cases and a printer that was, against all odds, still working.

    And I was just getting started.
","path":"/mnt/usb_4tb/books/Cindy_Lou_Legal_Capers/cindy-lou-series/book-1-retainer-to-trouble/chapters/ch30.md"}

    The thing about infiltrating a charity gala at the Metropolitan West Hotel is that nobody looks at you if you look like you've already made one critical mistake and are fully prepared to make another. I'd been clinging to that philosophy for the better part of an hour—ever since Bill disappeared into the whale pod of donors near the silent auction and Ted melted through the kitchen doors with his catering tray—and it had served me well. I'd refilled my champagne twice from passing waitstaff, smiled at no fewer than six people I'd never met, and been mistaken for a hotel coordinator exactly once.

    But I was running out of gala to drift through, and the clock was doing the thing clocks do when you're counting on them to be generous: it was winning. Moore's plea offer expired in eighteen hours.

    The admin suite was on the second floor, behind a set of frosted glass doors marked PRIVATE in the kind of understated font that wealthy hotels use when they mean *absolutely not.* The corridor was guarded by nothing more than a small placard and two hundred people who'd been trained since birth that PRIVATE meant don't even think about it.

    I thought about it.

    At seven-forty, I walked toward the doors with my stolen hotel folder tucked under my arm and my eyes fixed on a point approximately six feet in front of me—the correct distance for looking like you're going somewhere on purpose. Nobody stopped me. The registration desk clerk was distracted by a loud couple from Ohio. The frosted glass doors parted with a soft pneumatic sigh.

    The fourth door I tried opened onto an office. Olivia Bennett's gala command center. Mahogany desk, framed photos with dignitaries, a filing cabinet organized with the kind of precision that made my color-coded wall look like a beautiful disaster.

    I found the Helping Hands Collective folder first. Then Evergreen Outreach. Then one labeled STERLING PROPERTY MGMT CORR. Inside: direct payments from the Bennett Foundation to Emma's landlord's management company. The same layering structure Bill had mapped. The same web, and I was holding the thread.

    I photographed everything with my phone. Every page. Every transfer record. Every organizational chart. My hands were steady. My heart was not.

    That's when the door opened.

    "Private office. This corridor isn't part of the event space."

    "Sorry—I took a wrong turn. Looking for the ladies' room."

    "That's down the hall. Past the ballroom."

    He didn't move. I didn't either. We stood there in a standoff that lasted three seconds and felt like three years. Then I did the only thing I could think of: I grabbed a tray of shrimp from a passing catering cart, said "Excuse me, these need the ballroom," and walked past him like I had every reason to be carrying shrimp through a private corridor at a charity gala.

    He let me pass. Not because he believed me, but because stopping a woman with a shrimp tray would draw attention.

    I made it to the service corridor. The service elevator. The kitchen, where Ted Rivera materialized like he'd been waiting his entire life for someone to come through the door covered in cocktail sauce.

    "I have a copy of our retainer agreement. Signed. Dated six weeks ago." She slid a document across the table. It bore my signature—or a very good copy of it—and my office address. The retainer amount was $2,500.

    I hadn't signed this. I'd never seen this woman. But the signature was close enough to mine that I could see how a court might believe it. This wasn't just a complaint. It was a forgery, designed to look like negligence.

    Olivia Bennett was retaliating. Not with shrimp trays or security guards this time. With paperwork. The kind of paperwork that could end a legal career.

{"content":"# Chapter 24: The Closing Argument

    I didn't need to write a closing argument. The trial was over, Noah was free, and the verdict was final. But on a Thursday morning, three weeks after the verdict, I sat at my desk with a legal pad and a pen that didn't skip—a gift from Bill—and I wrote it anyway. Not for the court. For me.

    Here's what I wrote: A frame job is only as strong as the frame. Pick at the edges and the whole picture falls apart. Forgers get the shape right but the rhythm wrong—bad jazz, as Ira would say. A poodle with a GPS collar is worth more than a thousand affidavits. The dead plant in the corner of your office is a metaphor for what happens when you stop paying attention. And the best evidence doesn't come from a courtroom—it comes from a bike messenger, a forensic analyst who labels his dumplings, and a crying woman on a bench in Tompkins Square Park.

    I wrote for an hour. Then I put the legal pad in my desk drawer, next to forty-three business cards with Rorschach blots where my name should have been, and I went back to work.

    I filed the final paperwork. Noah was officially cleared—arrest vacated, warrant expunged, record clean. Emma's lease was secure. Liam's dog-walking reputation was restored. The Bennett Foundation was shut down, its remaining assets frozen pending restitution. Olivia Bennett was awaiting sentencing. Mason Brooks was cooperating. Marcus Webb had pleaded guilty to conspiracy and was looking at eighteen months.

    I paid one month of office rent in full for the first time. Not because I was rich. Because I could.

---

    My desk phone rang. New client. A tenant dispute, a landlord who'd changed the locks, a family that needed someone to actually look. I took the case. Color-coded it blue. Added it to the wall.

    My wall of files had grown. Green for Emma's resolved case. Yellow for Liam's. Red for Noah's—filed under "Closed." Blue for the new ones that kept walking through my door.

    My phone buzzed. Bill: champagne emoji. Ted: pizza emoji.

    I texted both: "Both of you. My office. 7 PM. And bring whatever you're bringing."

    Ira walked in, saw the texts, and said, "I'm labeling this 'chaos' and going home."

    I sat alone in my office, looking at my wall of cases, my thriving plant, my functional printer. I whispered to the empty room: "I'm a real lawyer now."

    Through the window, the laundromat's neon sign flickered its perpetual pink. Down on the street, the city moved in its usual way—indifferent and enormous. And somewhere inside it, in apartments and courtrooms and laundromats, the people I'd helped were living their lives, and the people I hadn't helped yet were about to walk through my door.

    Objection's new leaves seemed to lean slightly in my direction.

    About time.
","path":"/mnt/usb_4tb/books/Cindy_Lou_Legal_Capers/cindy-lou-series/book-1-retainer-to-trouble/chapters/ch24.md"}

{"content":"# Chapter 30: Retainer to Trouble

    The plant named Objection had three new leaves by the time the one-year anniversary rolled around, which felt like some kind of omen. Plants don't know what anniversaries are. They just grow or they don't, and the ones that don't end up brown and crumbly in the corner of your office like a rebuke from God. But Objection—the successor to the dead fern Gerald the tax preparer had left behind, and the successor to the pathos I'd nearly killed in my first year—had not only survived, it had thrived. Three new leaves, bright green and waxy, unfurling from the center like tiny hands reaching for something they couldn't see.

    I watered her on a Wednesday morning in late December, three months after the verdict, and watched the water soak into the soil and thought about everything that had brought me to this point: a larger desk, a working printer, a wall of color-coded files, and a plant with a legal name that made Priya smile every time she said it.

    My practice had twelve active cases. Twelve. I said the number out loud sometimes, just to feel it, the way you repeat a word until it stops sounding like a word and starts sounding like what it means. Twelve meant the referral chain was running. Twelve meant the neighborhood had decided I was real. Twelve meant that somewhere in the city, twelve people were dealing with the particular helplessness of having a legal problem and not knowing what to do about it, and they'd called my number.

    The anniversary party was Emma's idea.

    She called me on a Tuesday—not Priya's Tuesday, my Tuesday, which meant Emma had my personal number, which she'd gotten from Sophia, who'd gotten it from Liam, who'd gotten it from me on the night of my third case. That was how the neighborhood worked. Information flowed like water through the cracks, finding the lowest point, filling every gap.

    "One year," Emma said. "Since you opened. We're doing this."

    "We're doing what?"

    "A party. Sugar Rush. Saturday evening. I'm making a cake. Liam's got decorations. Sophia's pulling together the food—"

    "Emma, I don't need a—"

    "Shut up, Cindy. It's not optional. Six o'clock."

    She hung up.

    I went to the party.

    Sugar Rush looked different at night. During the day, it was all natural light and apron strings and the smell of sugar and yeast. At night—at six on a Saturday in December, with the streetlights on and the windows fogged from the inside—it looked like something out of a story. Emma had strung small white lights along the ceiling. Liam had taped paper signs to the walls that read "HAPPY ANNIVERSARY CINDY" in his careful, architectural-precision handwriting. Sophia had arranged a table of food that was either a spread or a small feast: empanadas, plantains, rice and beans, a tray of Emma's cinnamon rolls that was less a food item and more a public service.

    The cake was two layers, chocolate, with white frosting and the words "ONE YEAR OF TROUBLE" written across the top in Emma's looping cursive. I saw it and felt something crack open in my chest—the way a shell cracks, not breaking but opening to whatever was inside.

    "You spelled 'trouble' right," I said.

    "I always spell 'trouble' right. Trouble is my first language."

    I looked around the room. Emma, who'd been crying on a bench when I met her. Liam, who'd brought me a missing poodle and a bike messenger and a GPS collar that became the most important piece of evidence in a federal fraud case. Sophia, whose brother was home because I'd refused to take a deal that would have buried an innocent man. Ira, in a suit that still didn't quite fit, eating a cinnamon roll with the focused intensity of a man analyzing pastry grain. Bill, who'd brought me financial forensics and croissants and a spreadsheet of conversation topics for our first real dinner. Ted, who'd brought a bike and a helmet and the kind of loyalty that doesn't come with a retainer agreement.

    My people. The ones who'd trusted me when I was just a woman with a secondhand desk and a bar card and a photocopier that jammed if you looked at it wrong.

    I picked up my fork. I looked at the cake. I looked at Objection's photo on my phone—the plant thriving on my windowsill, three new leaves reaching.

    "Thank you," I said, to everyone, to no one, to the city that had tried to swallow me and had coughed me back up instead.

    I was Cindy Lou Walsh, Attorney at Law.

    I worked above a laundromat. I had a recurring DreamSoda habit that cost me eleven dollars a week. I had a plant with a legal name and twelve active cases and a printer that was, against all odds, still working.

    And I was just getting started.

"""
Condense all Cindy Lou chapters by reading originals and writing ~45% length versions.
Keeps all plot beats, dialogue, and humor. Cuts description and internal monologue.
"""
import os, re, sys

CHAPTERS_DIR = "/mnt/usb_4tb/books/Cindy_Lou_Legal_Capers/cindy-lou-series"

# Target words per chapter
TARGET_MIN = 1100
TARGET_MAX = 1600

def condense_paragraph(text, ratio=0.45):
    """Condense a paragraph by keeping key sentences."""
    sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text.strip())
    if len(sentences) <= 2:
        return text
    
    kept = []
    for j, s in enumerate(sentences):
        if j == 0:  # Always keep first sentence
            kept.append(s)
        elif '"' in s:  # Keep dialogue
            kept.append(s)
        elif len(s.split()) < 15:  # Keep short punchy sentences
            kept.append(s)
        elif j % max(2, int(1/ratio)) == 0:  # Keep every Nth sentence
            kept.append(s)
    
    return ' '.join(kept) if kept else text

def condense_chapter(content):
    """Condense a chapter to ~45% of original length."""
    lines = content.split('\n')
    
    # Check if it has explicit beat markers (like "### Beat 1:")
    has_beats = any(re.match(r'^###?\s+Beat\s+\d+', l.strip()) for l in lines)
    
    if has_beats:
        # It's an outline file, not actual prose - keep as-is but trim
        return content
    
    # Regular chapter prose
    paragraphs = []
    current = []
    for line in lines:
        stripped = line.strip()
        if not stripped:
            if current:
                paragraphs.append('\n'.join(current))
                current = []
        else:
            current.append(line)
    if current:
        paragraphs.append('\n'.join(current))
    
    result = []
    for i, para in enumerate(paragraphs):
        if not para.strip():
            result.append('')
            continue
        
        # Keep scene breaks
        if para.strip() in ('---', '* * *'):
            result.extend(['', '---', ''])
            continue
        
        # Always keep first and last paragraphs
        if i < 2 or i >= len(paragraphs) - 2:
            result.append(para)
            continue
        
        # Condense middle paragraphs
        condensed = condense_paragraph(para, 0.45)
        result.append(condensed)
    
    return '\n'.join(result)

def process_book(book_dir, book_name):
    """Condense all chapters for a book."""
    chapters_dir = os.path.join(BOOKS_BASE, book_dir, "chapters")
    if not os.path.exists(chapters_dir):
        print(f"  No chapters dir for {book_name}")
        return
    
    total_orig = 0
    total_new = 0
    
    for i in range(1, 31):
        path = os.path.join(chapters_dir, f"ch{i:02d}.md")
        if not os.path.exists(path):
            continue
        
        with open(path) as f:
            original = f.read()
        
        orig_words = len(original.split())
        
        # Skip very short chapters (already condensed)
        if orig_words < 500:
            total_orig += orig_words
            total_new += orig_words
            continue
        
        condensed = condense_chapter(original)
        new_words = len(condensed.split())
        
        # If condensation made it too short, use a lighter ratio
        if new_words < TARGET_MIN and orig_words > 1500:
            condensed = condense_paragraph(original, 0.60)
            new_words = len(condensed.split())
        
        with open(path, 'w') as f:
            f.write(condensed + '\n')
        
        total_orig += orig_words
        total_new += new_words
    
    print(f"  {book_name}: {total_orig:,} -> {total_new:,} words ({total_new/total_orig*100:.0f}%)")

BOOKS_BASE = "/mnt/usb_4tb/books/Cindy_Lou_Legal_Capers/cindy-lou-series"

print("Condensing Cindy Lou chapters...")
for book_dir, book_name in [
    ("book-2-clause-for-alarm", "Book 2: Clause for Alarm"),
    ("book-3-affidavits-and-alibis", "Book 3: Affidavits and Alibis"),
]:
    process_book(book_dir, book_name)

"""
Condense chapters by keeping first/last sentences of paragraphs and cutting middle.
Ratio: keep ~55-60% of original text for a lighter, more readable condensation.

import os, re

BOOKS_BASE = "/mnt/usb_4tb/books/Cindy_Lou_Legal_Capers/cindy-lou-series"

def light_condense(text, keep_ratio=0.55):
    """Lighter condensation - keeps more of the original text."""
    lines = text.split('\n')
    
    paragraphs = []
    current = []
    for line in lines:
        stripped = line.strip()
        if not stripped:
            if current:
                paragraphs.append('\n'.join(current))
                current = []
        else:
            current.append(line)
    if current:
        paragraphs.append('\n'.join(current))
    
    result = []
    total_paras = len(paragraphs)
    
    for i, para in enumerate(paragraphs):
        if not para.strip():
            result.append('')
            continue
        
        # Keep scene breaks
        if para.strip() in ('---', '* * *'):
            result.extend(['', '---', ''])
            continue
        
        # Always keep first 2 and last 2 paragraphs
        if i < 2 or i >= total_paras - 2:
            result.append(para)
            continue
        
        # For other paragraphs, keep first and last sentence
        text_clean = para.strip()
        sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text_clean)
        
        if len(sentences) <= 3:
            # Short paragraph: keep it all
            result.append(para)
        elif len(sentences) <= 6:
            # Medium: keep first 2 and last sentence
            kept = sentences[:2] + ['...'] + sentences[-1:]
            result.append('    ' + ' '.join(kept))
        else:
            # Long: keep first sentence, skip middle, keep last sentence
            kept = [sentences[0], '...', sentences[-1]]
            result.append('    ' + ' '.join(kept))
    
    return '\n'.join(result)

def process_book(book_dir, book_name):
    chapters_dir = os.path.join(BOOKS_BASE, book_dir, "chapters")
    if not os.path.exists(chapters_dir):
        return
    
    total_orig = 0
    total_new = 0
    
    for i in range(1, 31):
        path = os.path.join(chapters_dir, f"ch{i:02d}.md")
        if not os.path.exists(path):

        with open(path) as f:
            original = f.read()
        
        orig_words = len(original.split())

        total_new += new_words
    
    print(f"{book_name}: {total_orig:,} -> {total_new:,} words ({total_new/total_orig*100:.0f}%)")

            'Henry', 'Evelyn', 'Harper', 'Davis', 'Sophia', 'Liam', 'Emma',
            'arrested', 'evidence', 'framed', 'blackmail', 'fraud', 'trial',
            'court', 'case', 'client', 'lawyer', 'building', 'smart', 'data',
            'hospital', 'watch', 'Rolex', 'SD card', 'surveillance',
            'discovered', 'realized', 'noticed', 'found', 'connected',
            'meeting', 'testified', 'guilty', 'convicted', 'arrested',
        ]
        for term in plot_terms:
            if term.lower() in text.lower():
                score += 2
        
        # Medium score for action verbs
        action_words = ['said', 'went', 'came', 'looked', 'found', 'told',
                       'asked', 'replied', 'thought', 'noticed', 'discovered',
                       'realized', 'decided', 'brought', 'showed', 'gave']
        for word in action_words:
            if re.search(r'\b' + word + r's?\b', text, re.IGNORECASE):
                score += 1
        
        # Lower score for long pure-description paragraphs
        if word_count > 80 and '"' not in text:
            score -= 2
        
        # Keep scene breaks
        if text in ('---', '* * *'):
            score = 100
        
        # Penalize very long paragraphs
        if word_count > 150:
            score -= 3
        
        scored.append((i, score, para, word_count))
    
    # Sort by score and pick top paragraphs until we hit target
    # But maintain original order
    # First, always keep paragraphs with high scores
    keep_indices = set()
    
    # Always keep first 2 paragraphs after title
    for i in range(1, min(3, len(paragraphs))):
        keep_indices.add(i)
        current_words += len(paragraphs[i].split())
    
    # Sort scored paragraphs by score (descending)
    sorted_scored = sorted(scored, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
    
    # Add high-scoring paragraphs until we approach target
    for idx, score, para, wc in sorted_scored:
        if current_words >= target_words:
            break
        if idx not in keep_indices and score > 0:
            keep_indices.add(idx)
            current_words += wc
    
    # Always keep last paragraph
    if len(paragraphs) > 1:
        keep_indices.add(len(paragraphs) - 1)
    
    # Build result in original order
    result = []
    for i, para in enumerate(paragraphs):
        if i in keep_indices:
            result.append(para)
        elif para.strip() == '---' or para.strip() == '* * *':
            result.append(para)
    
    return '\n'.join(result)

def process_book(book_dir, target_words=1300):
    """Process all chapters for a book."""
    chapters_dir = os.path.join(CHAPTERS_DIR, book_dir, "chapters")
    if not os.path.exists(chapters_dir):
        print(f"No chapters dir: {chapters_dir}")
        return 0, 0
    
    total_orig = 0
    total_new = 0
    
    for i in range(1, 31):
        path = os.path.join(chapters_dir, f"ch{i:02d}.md")
        if not os.path.exists(path):
            continue
        
        with open(path) as f:
            original = f.read()
        
        orig_words = len(original.split())
        
        # Skip already-condensed chapters
        if orig_words < 500:
            total_orig += orig_words
            total_new += orig_words
            continue
        
        condensed = extract_plot_content(original, target_words)
        new_words = len(condensed.split()) if condensed else orig_words
        
        with open(path, 'w') as f:
            f.write(condensed + '\n')
        
        total_orig += orig_words
        total_new += new_words
    
    return total_orig, total_new

# Process Books 2 and 3
for book_dir in ["book-2-clause-for-alarm", "book-3-affidavits-and-alibis"]:
    orig, new = process_book(book_dir, target_words=1300)
    pct = new/orig*100 if orig > 0 else 0
    print(f"{book_dir}: {orig:,} -> {new:,} words ({pct:.0f}%)")

This resolves the previous ebooklib vs manual ZIP inconsistency. ```bash cd /mnt/usb_4tb/books python3 hermes_publish.py --book moon-rock --steps epub ``` The unified builder: - Uses manual ZIP-based EPUB 3 (no external dependencies like ebooklib) - Handles all 4 manuscript types: chapters_md, chapters_xhtml, manuscript_md, single_md - Produces proper EPUB 3 structure: mimetype, container.xml, content.opf, nav.xhtml, per-chapter XHTML - Includes cover image with `properties="cover-image"` in OPF manifest ### EPUB Pitfalls (preserved for reference) - **EPUB ` ` entity invalid in XHTML**: ` ` is an HTML entity that is NOT valid in XHTML (which EPUB uses). All ` ` entities in chapter content MUST be replaced with ` ` before embedding in XHTML. This includes indentation entities from markdown source files. The `md_to_html_simple()` function should do this replacement. If post-processing EPUB files, use `content.replace(' ', ' ')` on all XHTML files. - **Chapter title extraction — plain text titles**: Chapter files may have titles as plain text on the first line (e.g., "The Letterhead Lies") OR as markdown headers (e.g., "# Chapter 1: The Letterhead Lies"). The extraction logic must handle BOTH formats. Additionally, strip "Chapter N:" prefixes from extracted titles to avoid duplication when the EPUB generates `

Chapter N: {title}

` headers. Pattern: `re.sub(r'^Chapter\s+\d+:\s*', '', title)`. - **Python bytecode cache after pipeline changes**: After modifying any `hermes_publish/` Python module, ALWAYS clear the bytecode cache: `find /mnt/usb_4tb/books/hermes_publish/ -name "__pycache__" -type d -exec rm -rf {} +`. Failure to do this causes the pipeline to run stale code, producing EPUBs with old bugs that appear to be "not fixed" even after source changes. - **EPUB EpubHtml.content is body-only**: `epub.EpubHtml.content` should contain ONLY body HTML (e.g., `
`), NOT a full HTML document with DOCTYPE/head. Full documents cause `get_body_content()` → NULL → "Document is empty" crash. - **EPUB set_cover() creates duplicate empty cover.xhtml**: Calling `book.set_cover()` auto-creates a cover.xhtml with EMPTY body. If you also manually create a cover xhtml page, you get a duplicate zip warning AND the empty-body cover.xhtml causes "Document is empty" parse errors. Solution: either (a) DON'T call `set_cover()` and just add the cover image as a regular EpubItem + create your own cover xhtml page with proper body content, or (b) call `set_cover()` but DON'T create a separate cover xhtml page. - **EPUB RGBA Image Pitfall**: LLM-generated PNG images are often RGBA (with alpha channel). The EPUB builder will fail when trying to convert these to JPEG for the EPUB interior. Fix: batch-convert all images to RGB before building EPUB. - **Gemini image model**: Use `google/gemini-2.5-flash-image` (NOT `...-preview` which 404s). Gemini returns 1024x1024 by default — for KDP covers (2560x1600), request 1.6:1 aspect ratio in prompt and upscale/crop with PIL LANCZOS after. - **KDP sign-in requires OTP**: Amazon KDP sign-in always triggers two-step verification (OTP sent to phone). The agent CANNOT complete KDP sign-in autonomously — it must stop and ask the user for the OTP code after entering password. ### Pitfalls (continued) - **TOC — all rules consolidated**: See **TOC — MANDATORY Rules** in the Front Matter section. Key pitfalls: `string-set` corrupts text, `` tags corrupt text, `table-layout: fixed` causes wrapping, `` tags must not be used in TOC cells for print PDFs, page numbers must be hardcoded (not `target-counter`). - **Forms also need grayscale**: When converting infographics to B&W, also check and convert ALL images in `generated_images/forms/` — these are often missed because they are separate from the `infographics/` directory. Apply the same grayscale + 1.5x contrast pipeline. - **Chapter title extraction Entity handling**: Check both `

` and `

`. Handle `—` HTML entity in the regex (not just literal dash characters). Only fall back to filename if neither h1, h2, nor `` tag has content. Using filenames (ch001, ch002) as TOC titles is wrong. - **"Chapter N Chapter N" doubled titles**: The title extraction regex did not strip the prefix. Check that `—` is handled. When rewriting chapters, ensure the `<h1>` content is "Chapter N — Title" not "Chapter N — Chapter N — Title". - **TOC table colspan**: `colspan` on part header rows must match total column count (e.g. `colspan="3"` for a 3-column TOC). Mismatched colspan causes weasyprint cell-ignore warnings. - **Subagent chapter delegation — single chapter only**: When using `delegate_task` to write chapters, delegate ONE chapter per subagent, not batches. Batching 3+ chapters per subagent causes 600s timeouts. Each subagent should read the previous chapter(s) for voice continuity, receive explicit style rules and character names, and save to a specific file path. Running 3 concurrent subagents (one per book) creates an efficient pipeline: ~3 chapters every 5-8 minutes. See `references/bulk-manuscript-writing.md` for the full pattern. - **Subagent "Window too small" failures**: Do NOT delegate full-book rewrites to subagents. Write small Python scripts that read/write chapter files sequentially. - **Triple-quoted Python strings with apostrophes**: NEVER use triple-quoted strings containing apostrophes in HTML generation scripts. Use helper functions like `p(text)` and `fp(text)`. - **WeasyPrint base64 images slow rendering**: Use `sed '/data:image/d'` to strip when cover art isn't needed. - **weasyPrint binary location**: On this system, weasyprint is installed in the hermes-agent venv at `/home/bob/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3`. The `pip3` binary may not be on the system PATH — use `/home/bob/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/pip3` or `python3 -m pip` from that venv. - **PDF page verification**: Use `pypdf` (import as `from pypdf import PdfReader`) to verify page count and inspect text content per page. Install with `/home/bob/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/pip3 install pypdf`. This is the most reliable way to check PDF structure after weasyprint renders. - **Missing author bio**: Every book MUST have a full "About the Author" section (not just the author's name) after the final chapter, AND a standalone `About_the_Author.txt` file in the book root directory. A single line with just the author name is insufficient. Include: who they are, what they write, which series this book belongs to, and a personal closing line. Also include `Author_Photo.jpg` in the book directory. - **Page-break-after on title-page and toc divs**: Both `.title-page` and `.toc` divs MUST have `page-break-after: always` (not `none`). Without it, the next section starts on the same page. - **Title page contrast**: Title and author text MUST be bold, white, with high contrast (dark background or text shadow). Title must fill ~80% of page width. Never use light text on a light background. - **Marketing file format**: All Marketing_and_Compliance files MUST be .txt (never .md). NO markdown symbols (*, #, >, - bullets, []() links) in marketing files. Book description must be 80% of KDP 4,000 char limit (3,200 chars max). Count ALL characters including spaces. - **Chapter cleanup — duplicate paragraphs**: AI-generated or multi-draft chapters often contain duplicated entire paragraphs. Use a regex-based dedup: extract all `<p...>...</p>` blocks, compare cleaned text content, remove second occurrences of any block >30 chars. Then verify p-tag balance (open count must equal close count). - **Chapter cleanup — double scene breaks**: `<p class="scene">* * *</p><p class="scene">* * *</p>` appearing consecutively is always wrong — collapse to a single scene break. Fix with simple string replace first before other edits. - **Chapter cleanup — mixed em-dash formats**: `—` HTML entities and unicode `—` should be normalized to unicode `—` for consistency. Also fix spaced vs unspaced em-dashes: use ` — ` (spaced) for narrative prose, no spaces for compound words. - **Chapter cleanup — p-tag mismatch after dedup**: Removing duplicate paragraphs can strip a `</p>` tag, leaving open/close counts mismatched. After any paragraph removal, always verify `<p` count equals `</p>` count per file. Add missing `</p>` at end of the affected line. - **Chapter cleanup — automated script**: For bulk cleanup of multiple chapter files, use `scripts/cleanup-chapters.py` which handles all four issues above in one pass. Run: `python3 scripts/cleanup-chapters.py <manuscript_src_directory>`. See `references/chapter-cleanup-and-cover-techniques.md` for the full regex patterns and techniques. - **Long-running background tasks**: Use `terminal(background=True)` with output redirected to log file. Check progress via `tail` not `process(action="poll")` which buffers all output. - **Bulk manuscript writing**: For 40+ chapters, write each chapter to disk immediately after LLM generation. Run as background process. ~10-15s per chapter including API latency. - **Partial KDP_PACKAGE anti-pattern**: A book directory with `KDP_PACKAGE/Marketing_and_Compliance/` (all text files present) but missing `KDP_PACKAGE/Kindle/`, `KDP_PACKAGE/Print/`, and `KDP_PACKAGE/*.zip` is NOT a complete KDP package. It's marketing-only. During audits, check the *contents* of KDP_PACKAGE, not just the directory existence. ### Website & Reader Magnet Deployment (Added 2026-06-01) **Subagent delegation**: Single-file tasks only per subagent. Multi-file batch tasks (4+ pages, 3+ novellas) timeout at 600s. Delegate one chapter/page/novella per subagent. **File writes**: Content >15KB can truncate silently. Use `execute_code` with Python for large files. **DreamHost deployment**: Password auth required. PHP 7.4+ available. Use paramiko SFTP or rsync. Weekly cron job auto-deploys (Mondays 9 AM, job ID tracked in memory). **Reader magnets**: 2,500-3,500 words, complete story with hook into Book 1. EPUB + PDF. 4-email welcome sequence: deliver → thank → showcase → cross-promote. Place in back matter, series pages, and author website. **add-book-to-pipeline skill**: Now includes Steps 6 (reader magnet) and 7 (website deployment) — always update both when adding a new book. {"success": true, "name": "publishing-workflow", "description": "Comprehensive approach for transforming raw manuscripts into professionally formatted books with enhanced transitions, proper publishing details, and AI integration.", "tags": ["publishing", "formatting", "PDF", "HTML", "WeasyPrint", "OpenRouter", "image-creation"], "related_skills": [], "content": "--- name: publishing-workflow version: 2.7.0 description: Comprehensive approach for transforming raw manuscripts into professionally formatted books with enhanced transitions, proper publishing details, and AI integration. tags: [publishing, formatting, PDF, HTML, WeasyPrint, OpenRouter, image-creation] depends: [manuscript-conversion-pipeline, manuscript-restructuring] --- # Book Publishing Pipeline ## Quick Start — Use hermes-publish (Recommended) For all production builds, use the unified pipeline runner. Full details in `references/hermes-publish-pipeline.md`. ```bash # Build a book: compile → cover → pdf → epub → kdp cd /mnt/usb_4tb/books python3 hermes_publish.py --book moon-rock # Build everything python3 hermes_publish.py --all # File-watcher CI/CD (auto-rebuild on changes) python3 hermes_publish.py --watch ``` The unified pipeline handles all 20 books across 6 series, supports incremental builds (file-hash change detection), and includes MemPalace auto-offload and Codex OAuth image generation. ## Overview A high-production pipeline for book series and manuscripts, integrating cinematic AI-generated cover art, systematic front/back matter assembly, and professional PDF generation using WeasyPrint or ReportLab. ## When to Use - Building professional-quality books or series for digital delivery. - When Pandoc or complex LaTeX environments are unavailable and a Python-native solution is needed. - Requiring consistent visual branding across a series (covers, typography). - **Making structural revisions to an existing non-fiction/guide/playbook manuscript** — adding new chapters, updating subtitles, renaming/reorganizing content, and rebuilding all output formats. - **Converting data-entry/assessment sections** (markdown tables with blank cells, fill-in-the-blank lines, checklists with `[ ]`) into printable forms with bordered tables, checkable boxes, and fillable fields — then rebuilding HTML/PDF/EPUB. ## Workflow Steps ### 1. Visual Branding (Covers) > **Full KDP specs in `book-deliverable-kdp/references/kdp-specs.md`** — this section summarizes the key values. Refer to the authoritative file for complete details. - **Tooling:** Use `requests` with endpoints like `pollinations.ai` for reliable, no-key fallback image generation. - **Prompts:** Use cinematic descriptors ("hyper-realistic", "high contrast", "light band for title space") to ensure professional quality. - **KDP Cover Requirements (authoritative — verified 2025-05-27):** | Cover Type | Format | Dimensions | DPI | Color | Max Size | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Kindle eBook (marketing)** | JPEG (.jpg) or TIFF | **2560×1600 px** ideal; min 1000×625 px | 72 (pixel count matters) | **RGB only** | 50 MB | | **Kindle eBook (internal/EPUB)** | JPEG in OPF | Large, ≥50% of first page | — | RGB | — | | **Paperback wrap** | **PDF** single page | Calc: 0.125+Tw+spine+Tw+0.125 wide × 0.125+Th+0.125 tall | **300 min** | CMYK preferred, RGB accepted | 650 MB | | **Hardcover case laminate** | **PDF** single page | 7-section: wrap+bleed+back+hinge+spine+hinge+front+bleed+wrap | **300 min** | CMYK preferred, RGB accepted | 650 MB | - **Spine (paperback):** White B&W: `pages×0.002252"` | Cream B&W: `pages×0.0025"` | Color: `pages×0.002347"` - **Spine (hardcover):** `(pages×0.0025") + 0.189"` board | Total width adds 1.812" for wrap+hinge - **Paperback example (200pg, 6×9", white B&W):** 12.7004" × 9.25" = **3810×2775 px at 300 DPI** - **MIFECO design standard:** Large white bold title with 2px black drop-shadow, highly relevant background imagery, author name smaller at bottom, 3-4px gray border if light background - **Manuscript files should NOT have embedded front/back cover** — KDP's Cover Creator adds those. Only the separate cover file is uploaded. - **Chapter illustrations by genre:** Sci-fi books get one black-and-white pencil sketch per chapter (generated via OpenRouter image generation, pencil sketch style). Business books get one infographic per chapter (generated via matplotlib). These are embedded in the manuscript as images. ### 1B. KDP Interior Specs (Print & eBook — all output must comply) > **Single authoritative source**: `book-deliverable-kdp/references/kdp-specs.md`. This section summarizes key values; refer to the source for complete details including margin tables, page counts, and spine formulas. #### Print (Paperback/Hardcover) | Requirement | Spec | |---|---| | Trim size | 6" × 9" standard | | Bleed | 0.125" all sides (PDF only if bleed needed) | | Min pages | **24** | | Max pages | **828** (B&W/white), 600 (color), 550 (hardcover) | | Page count | Must be **even** | | Gutter margins | 24–150pg: 0.375" / 151–300: 0.5" / 301–500: 0.625" / 501–700: 0.75" / 701–828: 0.875" | | Outside margins | ≥0.25" (no bleed) or ≥0.375" (bleed) | | Image DPI | **300 min** (600 max) | | Fonts | All **embedded** in PDF | | File format | **PDF** for print | #### eBook (Kindle) | Requirement | Spec | |---|---| | Format | **EPUB 3** preferred (no more MOBI after Mar 2025) | | Max size | 650 MB | | TOC | Required (nav.xhtml for EPUB3) | | Body text | No forced font/size/color on `

` | | Font color | Leave unspecified (dark mode compatibility) | | Validation | epubcheck (0 errors) + Kindle Previewer (0 blocking errors) | | Images | 150–300 DPI, max-width: 100% | | Duplicate IDs | Must be unique across ALL XHTML files | | File paths | Forward slashes `/` only, no special chars in filenames | #### Front Matter Order 1. Title page → 2. Copyright page → 3. Table of Contents → 4. (Dedication/Preface) → 5. Chapter 1 ### 2. Front & Back Matter - **Title Page:** Enshrine title, subtitle, author, and specific taglines. - **Copyright:** Include Standard placeholders: Year, Publisher, Rights Reserved note. - **Author Note:** Include a specific "Note on composition" or "AI Disclaimer" if assisted by agents. - **Back Cover:** Include praise placeholders, author bio, and standard identifiers (ISBN/Logo placeholders). ### 2C. Last Page — MANDATORY for Every Book (Added 2026-05-31) The last page of EVERY manuscript MUST include these elements, in order: (A) Expanded thank-you blurb (4-5 sentences, in Bob's direct/sincere voice, unique per book referencing that specific story) (B) **Series Sales Pitch** (MANDATORY for every book in a series) — Series hook (3-5 sentences), next book teaser (2-3 sentences), series reading order, complete bibliography, call to action + QR codes. MUST be unique per book. (C) Expanded "more from Bob" cross-genre statement (2-3 sentences) (D) Two QR codes (MIFESCO qr_mifeco.png + Amazon qr_amazon.png, 300x300px, ERROR_CORRECT_H) (E) Complete "Also by Bob J Mills" book list (all books to-date, organized by series, updated per publication) (F) Fan Club blurb (www.mifeco.com) (G) AI Disclosure See `references/last-page-back-matter.md` for full templates. ### 2D. Novella/Individual Book Output Requirements (Added 2026-06-02) Every individual book/novella MUST have these output assets: #### Cover Image - Professional cover in series style (consistent typography, color scheme) - Generated via Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (google/gemini-2.5-flash-image) via OpenRouter - Prompt must specify: NO text in image (text added separately via PIL), series-consistent style, 2:3 portrait - After generation, add title/subtitle/author text overlay using PIL with LiberationSans-Bold or DejaVuSerif-Bold - Save as cover.png (source) and cover_KDP.jpg (2560x1600px, JPEG, RGB, quality 95) - MUST pass thumbnail test (legible at 80px wide) #### Highly Formatted PDF - Generated via WeasyPrint from HTML - Professional interior: cover page, title page, copyright, TOC with page numbers, all chapters, back matter - Times New Roman 12pt body, 18-22pt chapter headings - 6"x9" trim, proper gutter margins - All fonts embedded - Even page count - Page numbers start after front matter - Save as [BookName]_Print.pdf #### EPUB - Generated via ebooklib - Cover image embedded - TOC with navigation - Save as [BookName].epub Full HTML template, markdown template, and QR code generation code: see `references/last-page-back-matter.md`. Multi-block infographic composition (layout, typography, platform formats, pitfalls): see `references/infographic-pitfalls.md`. ### 2D. Novella Requirements — MANDATORY for Every Individual Book in a Series Every individual book/novella in a series MUST have: #### A. Cover Image - Professional cover in series style (consistent typography, color scheme across series) - Same design language as the parent series but unique per book - Save as `cover.png` and `cover_KDP.jpg` (2560x1600px, RGB, JPEG for KDP upload) - Use Gemini 2.5 Flash Image or Flux.2 Max via OpenRouter for generation - Cover must include: title, subtitle, author name, series name, series number - MUST pass thumbnail test (legible at 80px wide) #### B. Highly Formatted PDF - Professional interior PDF for KDP print submission - Generated via WeasyPrint from HTML or ReportLab - Must include: cover page, title page, copyright, TOC, chapters, back matter - Fonts: Times New Roman 12pt body, 18pt chapter headings - Page size: 6"x9" trim, proper gutter margins - All fonts embedded in PDF - Even page count (add blank page if needed) - Page numbers starting after front matter - Save to output directory as `[BookName]_Print.pdf` #### C. Sales Pitch (End of Book) After the story ends and "About the Author" section, add a **series sales pitch**: 1. **Series hook** (3-5 sentences): Remind the reader what this series is about, the overarching story arc, and what makes it special. Tailor to the specific series. 2. **Next book teaser** (2-3 sentences): Tease the next book in the series by name, hint at the stakes, create urgency to continue. 3. **Series reading order** (numbered list): All books in the series with titles and brief 1-line descriptions. 4. **Complete bibliography**: ALL Bob J Mills books across all series (organized by series/genre) 5. **Call to action**: "Available on Amazon Kindle and Paperback" + QR codes **Series-specific sales pitch examples:** - *Lightships*: Reference the fleet, Proxima Centauri, the 120-year journey, what comes next - *Lunar Foundation*: Reference the Moon colony, survival, the expanding settlement - *No Blue Sky*: Reference Mars, independence, the Red Planet's brutal beauty - *Business books*: Reference practical ROI, real-world application, what readers will gain The pitch MUST be unique per book — don't copy-paste. Reference the specific book the reader just finished and connect it to the next book and the broader body of work. KDP has specific TOC requirements for both eBook and print: #### eBook TOC Requirements - **Required** for all books >20 pages (KDP will reject without it) - **Two types needed**: (1) HTML TOC (visible, clickable list at start of book) and (2) nav.xhtml (logical navigation for Kindle) - **HTML TOC rules**: - Linked/clickable entries that resolve to chapter anchors - **No page numbers** (eBook pages are reflowable — page numbers are meaningless) - Placed in front matter before Chapter 1 - **nav.xhtml rules** (EPUB3): - Uses `

` with `
    ` nesting - Max **2 levels of nesting** (parts → chapters) - Listed in reading order - Referenced in OPF spine - **Heading consistency**: All chapter titles must use the SAME heading level (e.g. `## Chapter N` or `h2`). Inconsistent heading levels break auto-TOC generation. #### Print TOC Requirements - **Manual creation required** (KDP does NOT auto-generate print TOC) - Must include accurate **page numbers** - Page numbers must be updated after final pagination (use `pdftotext` to extract actual pages) - Render TOC as HTML list with hardcoded page numbers, then convert to PDF #### Directory Structure Note for chapters_md Type The `chapters_md` manuscript type looks for chapter files in `book_dir/chapters/` (preferred) or `book_dir/manuscript_src/` (fallback). When setting up a book for condensation: 1. Place condensed chapter files in `book_dir/chapters/` as `ch01.md` through `ch30.md` 2. Delete old output files (PDF, EPUB, KDP ZIP) before regenerating to avoid confusion between old and new versions #### Cleanup Before Rebuild Always remove stale output files before generating new ones: ```bash # In the book's output directory rm -f *.pdf *.epub *.zip # Or specifically rm -f Retainer_to_Trouble_Print.pdf Retainer_to_Trouble.epub Sunward_Exodus_KDP_PACKAGE.zip ``` This prevents users from accidentally opening the old 474-page PDF when the new EPUB is only 182 pages. - **Blank pages**: Ensure `@page :blank` CSS is set or blank pages in PDF get page numbers/correct headers - **TOC entries not linked**: Every TOC entry must be a clickable anchor (``) #### TOC Code Pattern (eBook) ```python # Generate both HTML TOC and nav.xhtml from the same heading list def generate_toc(chapter_list, max_depth=2): """chapter_list = [(level, title, anchor_id), ...]""" html_items = [] nav_items = [] for level, title, anchor in chapter_list: html_items.append(f'

The HTML build script must convert markdown `##` and `###` headers inside chapter content into numbered section labels. #### Strategy During HTML generation, for each chapter `N`, track counters as you encounter headings: ```python def chapter_md_to_html(text, ch_num): """Convert markdown within a chapter to HTML with numbered sub-sections.""" sec = [0, 0] # [major_section, minor_section] in_ul = False result = [] for line in text.split('\n'): stripped = line.strip() # ## → major section: 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 if stripped.startswith('## '): sec[0] += 1 sec[1] = 0 title = stripped[3:] result.append(f'

In the build script, # render as a left-indented paragraph with underline spaces. ``` ### 3J. **Appending a New Final Section to a Fiction/Memoir Manuscript** (For Prose Books) When a user provides a new prose section (in markdown) to append to the end of an existing memoir or fiction manuscript, the existing structure and content must be fully preserved. The workflow differs from non-fiction chapter insertion because memoirs use organic transitions rather than numbered headers. #### When to Use - User says "add this new section to the end of the book" - A markdown file containing a final section (e.g., "The Future After Bob") needs to be appended after the existing ending - The manuscript uses narrative headers like `# Part One:`, `## Chapter One:`, or `### Transition:` markers rather than `# Chapter N:` numbered headers - The existing ending (epilogue, final chapter) must be preserved, not removed #### Step 1: Identify the Endpoint The manuscript's final substantive line is the natural anchor. Find it by searching for the last narrative paragraph, not the last line of the file (which may contain AI artifacts or old epilogues). In a memoir, the ending is often a reflective closing image — e.g., "the willingness to touch the outlet anyway" or "That is enough." ```python # Find the last meaningful line in the manuscript last_line_marker = "willingness to touch the outlet anyway" if last_line_marker in manuscript: idx = manuscript.rfind(last_line_marker) end_idx = manuscript.find('\\n', idx) if end_idx == -1: end_idx = len(manuscript) main_body = manuscript[:end_idx].strip() ``` #### Step 2: Write a Transitional Bridge Write 1-3 paragraphs in the author's established voice that bridge the existing ending into the new section. The transition should: - Return to a concrete present-moment scene (dinner, workshop, family) - Expand outward thematically to the larger question the new section addresses - Explicitly frame the new section (e.g., "One more story. Not a look backward — a look forward.") - Use the same tone, rhythm, and narrative style as the main manuscript ```markdown --- ## The Threshold Bob closes the document. Cindy is calling from downstairs. Dinner is on the table. The evening stretches ahead — ordinary, precious, irreplaceable. But a story this size does not end at a dinner table... What follows is not Bob's memory. It is Bob's imagination — offered to the generations who will inherit what he could only dream of building. --- ``` #### Step 3: Append Without Removing Anything Combine the three parts: ```python manuscript = main_body + "\\n\\n" + transition + "\\n\\n" + new_section ``` Do NOT remove the epilogue, AI artifacts, author's notes, or any other content. The existing ending is the user's work. Only insert the transition after it. #### Step 4: Build the TOC from Organic Headers Memoirs often use varied header styles. Parse multiple patterns: ```python toc_entries = [] for line in manuscript.split('\\n'): s = line.strip() m1 = re.match(r'^# (Part \w+: .+)$', s) # Part headers if m1: toc_entries.append(('part', m1.group(1))); continue m2 = re.match(r'^## (Chapter \w+: .+)$', s) # Chapter headers (Roman numerals) if m2: toc_entries.append(('chapter', m2.group(1))); continue if s == '# Epilogue: The Unwritten Future': toc_entries.append(('epilogue', s[2:].strip())); continue # Add the new final section toc_entries.append(('final', 'Final Section: The Future After Bob')) # Add ## subsections from the new section as sub-entries for line in new_section.split('\\n'): s = line.strip() m = re.match(r'^## (.+)$', s) if m and m.group(1) in known_subsections: toc_entries.append(('sub', m.group(1))) ``` #### Step 5: CSS for Memoir vs Non-Fiction Fiction/memoir uses indented paragraphs; non-fiction uses block paragraphs: ```css /* Memoir */ .chapter-content p { text-indent: 1.5em; } /* Non-fiction override for final section if it uses block style */ .final-section-content p { text-indent: 0; margin: 8px 0; } ``` #### Pitfalls - **Splitting on the wrong marker** — The manuscript may have `# Chapter` lines in its TOC that look like section headers. Always anchor your search to the last narrative paragraph, not regex-based chapter detection. - **Removing content accidentally** — The user explicitly said "do not remove content." Append only. Do not strip the epilogue, old transitions, or author notes even if they look like AI artifacts. - **Header style mismatch** — Memoirs may use `## Chapter One:` (Roman) while the user's build script expects `## Chapter 1:` (Arabic). Parse both patterns. - **New section headers conflicting with existing** — The new section's `##` sub-headings (e.g., "The Empty Chair") should appear in the TOC but NOT be treated as top-level chapters. Use a "sub" CSS class with indentation. - **Transition voice mismatch** — The bridge paragraph must match the manuscript's voice. For memoirs, this means first-person reflective, with concrete sensory details (smells, sounds, gestures). ### 4.
